title: fix: bound value nesting on RDB/RESTORE decode, property writes and bulk insert
body: Closes #3338 ## Problem `GRAPH.RESTORE` decodes nested `T_ARRAY` values recursively (`Value::decode` in `graph/src/runtime/value.rs`) with no depth limit. A crafted payload with ~60,000 nested arrays exhausts the stack and aborts the server (SIGSEGV). Reproduced on a release build of `main` (8a66c01e5): depth 1,000 restores, depth 60,000 kills the server. ## Fix A shared constant `MAX_VALUE_NESTING = 4096` (plus `value_nesting_error()`) in `graph/src/runtime/value.rs`, enforced where a nested value enters storage: - **RDB / GRAPH.RESTORE decode**: `decode_value(r, depth)` counts depth and, on entry, returns a decode error for a value inside more than 4,096 arrays. Nothing recurses past 4,097 frames. - **Property writes** (`validate_list_property` in `pending.rs`): a list property nested past the cap is refused with `Property values can only be nested up to 4096 levels deep`. Lists can be built arbitrarily deep at runtime (e.g. `reduce(a = 1, i IN range(1, n) | [a])`), so this is checked when a value is stored, not at parse time. Every stored value can therefore always be saved and loaded back. This also covers the stored-value side of public issue #2722. - **GRAPH.BULK INSERT** (`read_property`): the iterative array reader refuses arrays past the cap. The values it built were otherwise walked recursively everywhere else. The effects (replication) decoder stays iterative and uncapped, as its comment explains. Its 5,000-level unit test is unchanged and passes. **Known trade-off:** an existing RDB that already holds a list property nested deeper than 4,096 levels will be refused on load. ## Choosing the cap On a release build, building and then freeing a nested list on a 2 MiB thread (the query pool's stack) survives about 25,900 levels (measured). 4,096 is a wide margin below that and far beyond any nesting real data uses. The new tests run the decoder, encoder, property validation and drop at exactly 4,096 levels on a thread spawned with a 2 MiB stack. ## Tests - Unit (`value.rs` `nesting_tests`): - decode at 4,096 succeeds and 4,097 errors; - a 60,000-deep payload returns an error; - an encode → decode round trip at 4,096, including drop, runs on a 2 MiB-stack thread. - Unit (`pending.rs` `property_nesting_tests`): a property at 4,096 is valid, 4,097 is refused, and the existing errors are unchanged. - Flow (`tests/flow/test_rdb_load.py`): - a real `GRAPH.RESTORE` payload, captured from `GRAPH.COPY`, with the property spliced to depth 10 / 4,096 restores; - 4,097 and 60,000 return an error, the key is not created, and the server answers PING; - nested list properties survive `DEBUG RELOAD`; - a list built to 4,096 levels with `reduce` is stored on a node and a relationship and survives `DEBUG RELOAD`; one level deeper is refused by CREATE and SET on both. **Before (origin/main + the new tests):** - `rdb_decode_refuses_one_past_the_cap` and `a_property_past_the_cap_is_refused` fail: the value is accepted. - `rdb_decode_refuses_the_advisory_payload` aborts the test process: the stack overflows. - Flow `test_restore_refuses_nesting_past_the_cap` fails: the payload restored and the key exists. The crashing inputs were not run against an unfixed server. **After:** - All new unit tests pass. - `test_rdb_load` 6/6 (2 existing + 4 new), `test_encode_decode` 19/19, `test_persistency` 11/11, `test_bulk_insertion` 14/14 and `test_replication` 2/2 pass. - e2e + functions: 131 passed. - `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 504 passed, 1 failed (`batched_result_emitter::cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, which fails identically on origin/main and is unrelated). - fmt is clean; clippy reports no new warnings in touched code. ## Bench `DEBUG RELOAD NOSAVE` of 1,000,000 nodes, each with list properties (`tags: [..3 strings]`, `v: [i, 2i, [i, 'x'], 1.5]`), release build, 7 runs per side, two alternating rounds: | | median | min | |---|---|---| | base round 1 | 679 ms | 671 ms | | fix round 1 | 659 ms | 653 ms | | base round 2 | 647 ms | 644 ms | | fix round 2 | 681 ms | 653 ms | The difference is within run-to-run noise. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes a stack overflow in `GRAPH.RESTORE` and RDB loading where a crafted payload with ~60,000 nested arrays crashed the server. Adds a shared `MAX_VALUE_NESTING` (4096) cap, enforced wherever a nested value enters storage, so values deeper than the cap are refused with an error instead of recursing into a crash. - RDB/`GRAPH.RESTORE` decode, property writes, and `GRAPH.BULK INSERT` now reject values nested deeper than 4,096 levels. - Runtime-built lists that exceed the cap are refused by `CREATE`/`SET`, and the limit matches what the RDB encoder/decoder supports, so every accepted value round-trips. - Existing RDB files containing list properties nested deeper than 4,096 levels will fail to load. **Tests** - Unit and flow tests cover the cap boundary, the 60,000-deep crash payload, and where runtime-built nesting is accepted or refused. - The flow test that captures a real `GRAPH.RESTORE` payload now connects to the server the test actually uses, so it passes in CI where the server runs in a service container. Written for commit 8c2609fdc11687269333751ebd4394d22692c533. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Node and relationship properties support recursively nested lists up to 4,096 levels deep, including after saving and reloading data. * **Bug Fixes** * Values exceeding the nesting limit are rejected during property creation, updates, and data loading. The server remains responsive when handling excessively nested values. * Lists continue to reject NULL elements and non-primitive values, while top-level NULL properties remain valid.

title: fix: bound the nesting depth of UDF value conversion
body:
Closes #3337

Fixes uncontrolled recursion in UDF value conversion (GHSA-frmf-ffvc-mxx5).

## Problem

`js_to_value` (UDF result → engine value) and `value_to_js` (engine value → UDF argument) recursed once per nesting level with no limit. A UDF can build an arbitrarily deep array or object in a loop, or an array that contains itself. Converting it exhausted the query thread's stack and the server aborted with SIGSEGV. A UDF returning a 300,000-level array kills the server on `main`.

## Fix

Both conversions now carry a depth and return a query error past `MAX_UDF_VALUE_NESTING`:

```
UDF value nesting exceeds the maximum depth of 1024
```

The check covers arrays, plain objects (maps) and the path members in `js_to_value`, and lists and maps in `value_to_js`. A self-containing array hits the limit and errors instead of recursing forever.

**Why 1,024, and why the stack also grows:** 1,024 is far beyond any nesting real data uses. The cap alone does not keep every build within a 2 MiB worker stack, because each level holds QuickJS handles and an `rquickjs` frame. Measured on a 2 MiB thread with the cap lifted:

| Build | Deepest JS → engine | Deepest engine → JS | Stack per level |
|---|---|---|---|
| release | 2,344 | 3,984 | ~0.9 KB |
| ASAN (CI's debug profile, `opt-level = 2`) | 354 | 354 | ~6 KB |

So each conversion level also runs through `stacker::maybe_grow`, which moves onto a fresh 1 MiB heap segment when less than 128 KB of stack is left. The cap bounds the work; the stack growth means no build's frame size can turn the cap into an overflow.


| Query | `main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| UDF returning a 300,000-level array | server crashes | query error, server up |
| UDF returning a 300,000-level object | server crashes | query error, server up |
| UDF returning a self-containing array | server crashes | query error, server up |
| UDF returning a 1,024-level array | works | works |

## Tests

- New unit tests in `udf::type_convert::nesting_tests`, run on a 1 MiB thread:
  - array and object at the limit convert, and one level past it is an error;
  - `value_to_js` at the limit converts and round-trips, and one past is an error;
  - the advisory's 300,000-level array and a self-containing array are errors;
  - ordinary nesting round-trips.
- With the guard disabled, the three past-the-limit tests fail on their assertions (they get a value instead of an error). The 300,000-level case isn't run against unguarded code.
- New flow test `test_udf.py::test_deeply_nested_result_is_an_error`: 300,000-level array and object, a 1,025-level array and a self-containing array each return the error, the server answers PING after each, and depth 1,024 plus ordinary nested results still work. `test_udf` passes 47/47 on this branch.
- `cargo fmt --check` clean; clippy clean in the touched file; `cargo test -p graph --lib` 504 passed (the one failure, `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, fails the same way on `main`, #2922); `tests/test_e2e.py` + `tests/test_functions.py` 131 passed.

## Bench

UDF calls converting a small nested value, release builds, 16 clients, 20,000 queries, 3 alternating rounds (p50 / p99 ms):

| Query | `main` (8a66c01e5) | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN b.out()`, a small nested result | 0.207 / 0.575–0.679 | 0.207–0.215 / 0.607–0.615 |
| `RETURN b.id([1,[2,3],{a:[4,5]},'s'])`, nested argument and result | 0.207 / 0.535–0.599 | 0.207–0.223 / 0.575–0.639 |

Within run-to-run noise and redis-benchmark's latency-bucket resolution.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Deeply nested or cyclic JavaScript values now return a clear error when they exceed the supported nesting depth.

## Follow-up: stack growth (78385b2)

Within run-to-run noise (each p99 range overlaps).

title: fix: a parenthesised WHERE uses the index and NodeByIdSeek again
body: Closes #3331 Closes #3187 ## Problem Parentheses around a `WHERE` predicate, or around one of its conjuncts, turn off index and id lookups. Results are correct; only the plan is worse: - `WHERE (n.k = 7 AND n.s = 1)` and `WHERE (n.k = 7) AND n.s = 1` use **Node By Label Scan** instead of **Node By Index Scan** (#3331), with literals or parameters. - `WHERE (id(n) = 42)` uses **All Node Scan + Filter** instead of **NodeByIdSeek**, and `MATCH (a), (b) WHERE ((id(a) = 1) AND (id(b) = 2))` becomes a **Cartesian Product of two All Node Scans** (#3187). The parser keeps an `ExprIR::Paren` node for `( ... )`, which it needs while parsing (`(a < b) < c` is not a chain, `SET (n).x` must open with `(`, `((x))` collapses). The binder copied that node into the bound tree. The optimizer passes (`utilize_index`, `utilize_node_by_id`, filter push-down, Cartesian-to-hash-join) match on the filter root and on the children of a top-level `And`, so a `Paren` hid the predicate from all of them. ## Fix Fixed once in the binder (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs`), so no optimizer pass has to know about parentheses: - The binder drops the `Paren` wrapper. The tree shape already carries the grouping, so `(x)` binds to the same IR as `x`. - The binder merges a nested `And`/`Or` into a parent of the same operator. Both are associative, and operand order is kept, so `(a AND b) AND c` splits into all three conjuncts. Unchanged: column names (they come from the source text, so `RETURN (1 + 2)` is still named `(1 + 2)`), chained comparisons (the parser decides those), `NOT (NOT x)`, and `(a - b) - c` vs `a - (b - c)`. These were checked live against C and match. On a graph of 100k `:A` nodes with an index on `k` (#3331 repro), plus a graph of 1000 nodes for the id cases: | Query | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `WHERE n.k = 7 AND n.s = 1` | Node By Index Scan | Node By Index Scan | Node By Index Scan | | `WHERE (n.k = 7 AND n.s = 1)` | Node By Label Scan | **Node By Index Scan** | Node By Index Scan | | `WHERE (n.k = 7) AND n.s = 1` | Node By Label Scan | **Node By Index Scan** | Node By Index Scan | | `WHERE ((n.k = 7) AND (n.s = 1))` | Node By Label Scan | **Node By Index Scan** | Node By Index Scan | | `WHERE (n.k = $k AND n.s = $s)` | Node By Label Scan | **Node By Index Scan** | Node By Index Scan | | `WHERE (id(n) = 42)` | Filter ← All Node Scan | **NodeByIdSeek** | NodeByIdSeek | | `MATCH (a), (b) WHERE ((id(a) = 1) AND (id(b) = 2))` | Filter ← Cartesian(All Node Scan ×2) | **Cartesian(NodeByIdSeek ×2)** | Cartesian(NodeByIdSeek ×2) | Every result is the same in all three columns. ### Benchmark The #3331 repro (100k nodes), `GRAPH.RO_QUERY` latency in ms over 3000 runs after 100 warm-up runs, two rounds, macOS arm64 release build: | `MATCH (n:A) WHERE (n.k = 7 AND n.s = 1) RETURN count(n)` | p50 | p99 | |---|---|---| | Rust before | 1.935 / 1.935 | 2.098 / 2.129 | | Rust after | 0.221 / 0.221 | 0.251 / 0.258 | | C | 0.211 / 0.213 | 0.255 / 0.239 | Rust after is within run-to-run noise of C; the unparenthesised form measures 0.218–0.222 / 0.242–0.253 on both Rust builds. `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE` is the same on all three (16 MB). ## Tests - **Unit** (`planner::binder::tests`): `parentheses_bind_to_the_same_ir` checks that parenthesised and plain forms bind to identical IR. It covers nested parens, parameters, `(a AND b) AND c`, `OR` groups, `NOT (x IN ([..]))`, the two-id Cartesian case, a parenthesised pattern predicate `WHERE ((a)-->())`, and a `SET` expression. `parentheses_that_regroup_still_bind_differently` checks that grouping which changes meaning is kept: `(a OR b) AND c`, `a - (b - c)`, `(a < b) < c`. The first test fails with the fix removed; the second passes either way. - **Flow**: `test_index_scans.py::test_42_parenthesised_predicates_use_the_index` (literals, parameters, nested parens, `IN`) and `test_node_by_id.py::test_parenthesised_id_predicates` (single id, nested, range, the #3187 two-id Cartesian, with parameters) assert both the plan and the results. - On `main`: both fail, for example `'Aggregate\n Filter\n Node By Label Scan | (n:A)' should contain 'Node By Index Scan'` and `'Project\n Filter\n All Node Scan | (n)' should not contain 'All Node Scan'`. - With this PR: both pass. They also pass on the C module. - Related flow suites all pass: `test_index_scans` (39), `test_edge_index_scans` (30), `test_node_by_id` (4), `test_optimizations_plan` (32), `test_path_filter` (19), `test_query_validation` (51), `test_params` (13), `test_filters` (9), `test_graph_merge` (38), `test_bidirectional_traversals` (12). - TCK done list: 10140 steps passed, 0 failed. `test_e2e.py` + `test_functions.py`: 131 passed. - `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 503 passed. The one failure, `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, already fails on macOS (#2922). - `cargo fmt --check` passes, and clippy reports no warnings in `binder.rs`. #3327 (test-only) has reproductions for these two issues. Once this merges, they can move into the suites. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #3331 and #3187: parenthesized WHERE predicates no longer disable index scans and node-by-id seeks. The binder now strips the parser's `Paren` wrapper and splices nested `And`/`Or` into a parent of the same operator, so `(n.k = 7 AND n.s = 1)` and `(id(n) = 42)` bind to the same IR as their unparenthesised forms. A new `ExprIR::and_of`/`or_of` builds flat AND/OR trees across planner and optimizer passes, so filters stay flat after every rewrite. Paren handling is removed from the runtime and vectorised evaluator. - Parenthesized predicates now use the index and NodeByIdSeek. - Column names and chained comparisons are unchanged. - Added unit and flow tests covering literals, parameters, and nested forms. Written for commit d46f80088dc15c5489b71f83036506aedc230d4e. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Parenthesized predicates now behave consistently with equivalent unparenthesized expressions, including when using indexes and node ID lookups. * Nested conjunctions and disjunctions are handled consistently, while parentheses that change expression grouping continue to preserve that grouping. * Predicates combined from pattern attributes and `WHERE` clauses can still use indexes. * **Tests** * Added coverage for parenthesized index scans and node ID predicates, including parameterized queries, range conditions, and merged filters.

title: fix: enforce unique constraints by index lookup, not a label scan per entity (#3330)
body: Fixes #3330. ## Cause `Pending::check_node_constraint` / `check_edge_constraint` rebuilt a hash of every key in the label **once per written entity**, so a commit cost O(written × label size). A single `CREATE` cost O(label), and a bulk insert was quadratic. ## Fix The check now looks each written entity's values up in the constraint's supporting index, as C's `EnforceUniqueEntity` does: - Each `Commit` publishes its index documents before the next one runs (`commit_deferred_indexes`), so the index lags only the commit being checked. - Written entities are compared among themselves through a key set. - Index hits are re-verified against the private graph. An entity that was deleted, lost the label, or was re-valued in this commit does not count. Hits that are themselves written in this commit are skipped, since the key set already covers them. - Without an operational index, or for a value the index can't match exactly (arrays, ints that lose f64 precision, NaN, empty strings), the label is scanned **once for the whole commit**, not once per entity. Semantics are unchanged: the key is still `build_composite_key`, and NULL or absent properties still opt out. ## Numbers These are local release builds on Apple M-series, against the C module (`master`). The first table is the issue's repro. | | C | Rust before | Rust after | |---|---:|---:|---:| | nodes 1–5,000 | 56 ms | 3,101 ms | 16 ms | | nodes 5,001–10,000 | 71 ms | 6,408 ms | 12 ms | | nodes 10,001–20,000 | 148 ms | 26,047 ms | 20 ms | | single `CREATE` at 20k, p50 / p99 | 91 / 152 µs | 2,855 / 3,144 µs | 81 / 174 µs | At 200k nodes (20 batches of 10k, then 5,000 single-row queries each): | | C int | Rust int | C string | Rust string | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | load 200k | 3,269 ms | 335 ms | 408 ms | 369 ms | | `CREATE`, p50 / p99 | 90 / 161 µs | 81 / 159 µs | 73 / 130 µs | 81 / 160 µs | | `MERGE … SET` new, p50 / p99 | 1,019 / 1,238 µs | 93 / 154 µs | 982 / 1,172 µs | 93 / 153 µs | | `SET id` on existing, p50 / p99 | 114 / 148 µs | 91 / 154 µs | 89 / 129 µs | 84 / 150 µs | On Rust the constraint now costs nothing measurable. String `CREATE` with no constraint is 80 / 156 µs, the same as with one. The small remaining p99 gap to C on single string writes, and the memory difference, also show up with no constraint, so they are not part of this issue. The fix adds no persistent state, so memory is unchanged. ## Tests `tests/flow/test_constraint.py::testUniqueConstraintLookup` covers: - a bulk-insert time bound: 35 s before the fix, about 30 ms after, against a 10 s bound - SET onto an existing value, and swapping two values - delete or remove-label followed by re-create in the same query, plus re-adding the label - a duplicate created in an earlier commit of the same query - values that take the scan fallback - composite keys - edges The six semantic tests pass on both the old and the new module; only the timing test fails on the old one. The existing `test_constraint` flow tests (26) and `cargo test -p graph` pass. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes the quadratic unique-constraint check: commits previously rebuilt a hash of every key in the label once per written entity, so a commit cost O(written × label size). Unique checks now look each written entity's values up in the constraint's supporting index, as C's `EnforceUniqueEntity` does. **Details** - Written entities are compared among themselves via a key set, and index hits are re-verified against the graph so deleted, unlabelled, or re-valued entities don't count. - Without an operational index, or for values it can't match exactly (arrays, ints that lose f64 precision, NaN, empty strings), the label is scanned once per commit rather than once per entity. Strings containing NUL use the index, since the tag encoding escapes them. - Semantics are unchanged: the key is still `build_composite_key`, and NULL or absent properties still opt out. No persistent state is added. **Benchmarks and tests** - Inserting 10k nodes into a 10k-node label drops from ~26s to ~20ms; a single `CREATE` at 20k goes from ~3.1ms p99 to ~170µs, on par with C. - New flow tests cover duplicates within and across commits, SET collisions and value swaps, delete/remove-label reuse, scan-fallback values, composite keys, and edges. Written for commit aa7663b6f521f6ae5764e252322cecab60afe6ba. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Unique constraints are enforced consistently during bulk inserts, updates, value swaps, and changes involving deleted or relabeled entities. * Composite keys, relationship constraints, and values that require scan-based checks are handled correctly. * Mandatory-constraint checks apply only to affected entities that match the constrained label or relationship type. * **Performance** * Uniqueness checks can run more efficiently when supporting indexes are available.

title: fix: parse module-load arguments like C (case-insensitive, validated, refused on bad input)
body: Closes #3268 ## Problem Module-load arguments (`--loadmodule falkordb.so NAME VALUE ...`) were read by two parsers. redismodule-rs's `module_args_as_configuration` handled the fields registered in `redis_module!`, with case-sensitive names and `value == "yes"` for booleans. An ad-hoc loop in `graph_init` handled the rest, with no `ASYNC_DELETE` arm, plain `parse::()` and no rejection of unknown names or a trailing odd argument. So `CMD_INFO YES` turned telemetry off, `cache_size 10` and `ASYNC_DELETE no` were ignored, and invalid or unknown arguments loaded where C refuses to start. ## Fix There is now one parser, as in C's `Config_Init` (option (a) in the issue, plus Dvir's points): - `module_args_as_configuration` is off. `apply_module_args` (`src/commands/config_cmd.rs`) parses every pair in `graph_init`. Names are ASCII case-insensitive. - Run-time fields go through the same `validate_config_set` + `apply_config_set` as `GRAPH.CONFIG SET`, one pair at a time like C, with the same timeout cross-checks. - Load-only fields get C's `Config_Option_set` rules: - `CACHE_SIZE`, `THREAD_COUNT`, `OMP_THREAD_COUNT`: positive integer. - `NODE_CREATION_BUFFER`: non-negative integer. - `INDEX_WORKER_THREADS` (Rust-only): non-negative integer. - `IMPORT_FOLDER`: any string. - `TEMP_FOLDER`: must exist, be a directory and be writable, with C's messages. - A bad argument refuses the load. The reason is logged at `warning` level using C's texts: - `Encountered unknown configuration field 'FOO'` - `FalkorDB received N arguments, all configurations should be key-value pairs` - `Failed setting field 'X' with error: ...` - `The TIMEOUT configuration parameter should be removed when specifying TIMEOUT_DEFAULT and/or TIMEOUT_MAX` - **Deprecated but accepted.** The engine has no behaviour yet for these C configs: `ASYNC_DELETE`, `DELAY_INDEXING`, `DELTA_MAX_PENDING_CHANGES`, `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD`. They are validated, stored and reported by `GRAPH.CONFIG GET`. They also log `configuration field 'X' is deprecated and has no effect in this version; the value 'V' is accepted and ignored`. - **`BOLT_PORT`** is out of scope, as agreed. It is accepted and unused, as before, with no validation added. - `GRAPH.CONFIG GET/SET` is unchanged. The `graph.*` Redis module configs are still registered, so `graph.X` lines in redis.conf and `CONFIG GET/SET graph.X` still work. Each row starts a fresh `redis-server --loadmodule `, then runs `GRAPH.CONFIG GET`. C is `bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`. | Load args | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | `CMD_INFO YES` | `0` | `1` | `1` | | `CMD_INFO garbage` | loads, `0` | refuses | refuses | | `DELAY_INDEXING YES` | `0` | `1` | `1` | | `cache_size 10` | `25` (ignored) | `10` | `10` | | `ASYNC_DELETE no` / `async_delete no` | `1` (ignored) | `0` | `0` | | `timeout_max 7` | `7` | `7` | `7` | | `CACHE_SIZE 0` | loads, `0` | refuses | refuses | | `CACHE_SIZE 5000` | `5000` | `5000` | `5000` | | `THREAD_COUNT 0` | loads, auto (`11`) | refuses | refuses | | `MAX_QUEUED_QUERIES 0` | loads, `0` | refuses | refuses | | `FOO 1` | loads, ignored | refuses: `Encountered unknown configuration field 'FOO'` | refuses (same message) | | `CACHE_SIZE` (odd count) | loads, `25` | refuses: `FalkorDB received 1 arguments, all configurations should be key-value pairs` | refuses (same message) | ### Behaviour changes (need a release note) 1. **Stricter start-up.** The following now stop the server from starting, as they do on C: - a non-yes/no boolean - `CACHE_SIZE 0`, `THREAD_COUNT 0`, `OMP_THREAD_COUNT 0`, `MAX_QUEUED_QUERIES 0` - negative values for non-negative fields (e.g. `EFFECTS_COMPRESSION -1`) - `JS_HEAP_SIZE`/`JS_STACK_SIZE` below 1MB - an unknown name - an odd argument count `THREAD_COUNT 0` used to mean "auto". Leaving `THREAD_COUNT` out still gives the default, one thread per core. Rust's names are a superset of C's, so nothing valid on C is refused. 2. **Module arguments now win over `graph.*` in redis.conf.** I checked with `loadmodule CACHE_SIZE 10` plus `graph.CACHE_SIZE 5` in the same redis.conf: - Before: `GRAPH.CONFIG GET CACHE_SIZE` returned `5`. - After: it returns `10`, and so does `CONFIG GET graph.CACHE_SIZE`. A `graph.*` line with no matching module argument still applies (`5`). Runtime `CONFIG SET graph.VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT 88` still works. C has no `graph.*` configs, so this affects only Rust-only setups. This changes start-up only, so no runtime benchmark was run. ## Tests New `tests/flow/test_module_args.py` (spawn bucket in CI; added to `flow_tests_done.txt`): - `test01_defaults`: with no arguments, every config keeps its default. - `test02_accepted`: all accepted rows from the table, plus mixed-case names (`Thread_Count 3`, `max_queued_queries 5`, `node_creation_buffer 600` → 1024, `Vkey_Max_Entity_Count 0`, and a valid `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT`/`TIMEOUT_MAX` pair). - `test03_refused`: every refused row, plus `DELAY_INDEXING 1`, `OMP_THREAD_COUNT 0`, `JS_HEAP_SIZE 5`, a 3-argument odd count and the three TIMEOUT conflicts. `Env()` must fail to start. Locally, the test also starts `redis-server --port 0` directly and asserts that the server exits, that the log has the expected message, and that it has `initialization failed. Module not loaded`. - `test04_ignored_configs_logged`: the four ignored configs are accepted and stored, and each logs the deprecation line. Results: - New test on `main`: fails. The 9 mismatched accepted rows, every refused row (all loaded) and the missing deprecation log lines are all reported. - New test with this PR: 4/4 pass. - Existing flow suites with module args, all passing: `test_config` 20/20, `test_timeout` 14/14, `test_cache` 15/15, `test_pending_queries_limit` 3/3, `test_graph_info` 15/15, `test_load_csv` 18/18, `test_encode_decode` 19/19, `test_multi_writer` 2/2, `test_rdb_load` 2/2, `test_replication_states` 1/1. - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. - `cargo test -p graph --lib`: 499 passed. The one failure is the known `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (#2922, macOS). - `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets` are clean on the touched code. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Parses module-load arguments (`--loadmodule falkordb.so NAME VALUE ...`) the way C's `Config_Init` does, closing #3268. Names are now ASCII case-insensitive, values get the same validation as `GRAPH.CONFIG SET`, and an invalid value, unknown name, or odd argument count refuses the load instead of being silently ignored. The parse happens once in `graph_init`, via `apply_module_args` in `src/config.rs`; `config_cmd.rs` shares its validators and setter with `GRAPH.CONFIG SET`. All pairs are validated before any are applied, so a refused load leaves no partial configuration, and pairs are checked in order with the same timeout cross-constraints as C's one-pair-at-a-time `Config_Init`. **Behavior changes** - The server now refuses to start, as in C, on non-yes/no booleans, `CACHE_SIZE 0`, `THREAD_COUNT 0`, `OMP_THREAD_COUNT 0`, `MAX_QUEUED_QUERIES 0`, negative values, unknown names, and odd argument counts. - Module arguments now win over `graph.*` lines in redis.conf, since they are applied after them. - Deprecated C configs (`ASYNC_DELETE`, `DELAY_INDEXING`, `DELTA_MAX_PENDING_CHANGES`, `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD`) are accepted and stored, with a deprecation log line. - New flow test `tests/flow/test_module_args.py` covers accepted, refused, and deprecated arguments. Written for commit 7dfde9b16c64085a1e9be0cbbd538f68baade48a. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Module-load configuration arguments are applied after `graph.*` settings from `redis.conf`, so they take precedence. * Argument names are case-insensitive, and supported settings are validated when the module loads. * **Bug Fixes** * Invalid values, unknown settings, malformed argument lists, and incompatible timeout combinations now cause module loading to fail with an error. * Selected deprecated settings are accepted but ignored, with a notice logged.

title: perf(index): apply native-index writes once per unit of work
body: Closes #3306 The native index is now updated once per unit of work instead of once per graph write call. ## One index update per unit of work The graph's write paths no longer change the native index themselves. Each records its changes in a `PendingIndexWrites` buffer carried in the unit of work's `IndexDocs`, the struct that already holds its RediSearch documents. The owner applies it once: - a Cypher query at the end of each `Commit` segment (`Pending::commit`), so a later operator in the same query reads the writes, as it does through RediSearch; - a replicated effects buffer once per buffer (`effects::v3::apply`); - `GRAPH.BULK` once per token. The 14 graph write methods take `&mut IndexDocs` in place of the single RediSearch map they took, and fill the same map as before plus, with the `index-falkordb` feature, `docs.native`. The write functions in `graph_writes` take `&Graph` and the buffer. `PendingIndexWrites` and its module exist only with the feature, and `PendingIndexWrites::apply` takes the `FalkorDbIndex`. `IndexDocs` moves from `runtime::pending` to `index::index_docs` and is re-exported from `runtime::pending`. The buffer keeps changes in the order they were made and applies only the last change to each `(value, id)`, because one write step can add an entry and then remove it: `SET n.v = 5 DELETE n` stages the SET's add before the DELETE's remove. `FalkorDbIndex::merge` is replaced by `apply_writes`. --- ## Summary by cubic The native index is now updated once per unit of work instead of once per graph write call. Graph write paths no longer touch the native index. The `graph_writes` helpers take `&Graph` and return the `IndexChanges` one write makes, encoded and in order; the graph's write methods stage them into a `PendingIndexWrites` buffer carried by the unit of work's `IndexDocs`, which now lives in `index::index_docs` and is re-exported from `runtime::pending`. Owners apply the buffer through `Graph::apply_index_writes` (which calls `FalkorDbIndex::apply`): a Cypher query at the end of each `Commit` segment, a replicated effects buffer once per buffer, and `GRAPH.BULK` once per token. `GRAPH.BULK` and the replica publish both index kinds at once through `Graph::commit_index_docs`, replacing the old `BulkIndexDocs` wrapper. `PendingIndexWrites` is plain data (`extend`, `drain`, `clear`, `is_empty`); the index digests it. **Last change per tuple wins** Batching removes the per-call removes-then-adds ordering. `SET n.v = 5 DELETE n` stages `add (5, n)` then `remove (5, n)` in one batch, so the buffer collapses each `(value, id)` to its final change before a single batched remove and add per column, keeping the deleted node out of the index. Written for commit cf878b9dd73e518717dd18a66f2126dcdd2b6bfc. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Improved index consistency when graph changes are combined in a single operation, including updates followed by deletions. * Updated node and relationship indexes after attribute changes, label changes, deletions, and bulk imports. * Preserved unaffected indexed records when applying batches of graph changes.

title: fix: an inline write no longer fails while a queued write is matching
body: Closes #3093 ## Problem A queued write claimed `MvccGraph`'s write slot (a CAS) as soon as it started, while it was still a reader matching without the GIL. An inline writer that ran in that window (`MULTI/EXEC`, Lua, `GRAPH.EFFECT`, anything on the main thread) took the GIL and the write lock, found the slot taken, and failed with `another write is in progress, retry the query`. Its write was lost. It could not wait instead, because the queued writer cannot escalate until the inline writer releases the GIL. C commits the inline write. ## Fix This is option A from the issue: claim the slot at escalation. - `MvccGraph::fork` makes a private version without claiming the slot. `MvccGraph::claim(fork)` claims it and checks that the fork still extends the committed version (`Claim::Busy` / `Claim::Stale`). `write()` is unchanged (claim + fork) for writers that already hold the write lock. - `QuerySession::write_version` hands a reader session an unclaimed fork. A writer session claims immediately. `upgrade_to_write` claims the fork right after escalating, under the GIL and the write lock. So the slot is only ever held by a thread that holds the write lock, and an inline writer never finds it taken. - If an inline writer committed while the query was matching, the claim reports `Stale`. At that point nothing has been mutated in shared state, no index document has been published, and nothing has been replied, so the query is dropped and run again from the start: - `execute_query_write` (GRAPH.QUERY / GRAPH.PROFILE) loops on a fresh session. - `GRAPH.BULK` rebuilds its fork. - `GRAPH.RECORD` (debug) reports the error. - `abandon_write` and `finish_write` release the slot only if this session claimed it (`QuerySession::release_slot`). `MULTI; GRAPH.QUERY mr "CREATE (:M)"; EXEC` sent 0.3 s after a queued `UNWIND range(1,40000000) AS x WITH count(x) AS c CREATE (:N {c:c})` (release build): | | MULTI reply | final counts | |---|---|---| | Rust before (`main` @ b033aecc6) | `another write is in progress, retry the query` (2/2 runs) | `N=1, Seed=1`, **M missing** | | Rust after | `Labels added: 1, Nodes created: 1` (3/3 runs) | `M=1, N=1, Seed=1` | | C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release`) | `Labels added: 1, Nodes created: 1` | `M=1, N=1, Seed=1` (C also crashed on 2 of 3 runs of this race, a separate C bug, as noted in the issue) | The queued write still commits exactly once (`N=1`). ## Tests - New flow test `test_multi_exec.py::test_write_while_queued_write_matches`. It runs MULTI while a queued write is matching and asserts that the inline write commits, that the queued write commits exactly once, and that the two really overlapped. - Before: `FAIL True == False [another write is in progress, retry the query]` and `[['N', 1], ['Seed', 1]] == [['M', 1], ['N', 1], ['Seed', 1]]`. - After: PASS. - `tests/test_concurrency.py::_multi_write` no longer swallows `another write is in progress`. A MULTI write under concurrent queued-write load must now succeed. - New unit test `mvcc_graph::tests::a_fork_is_claimed_late_and_refused_once_stale`. - Also run: - `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy` (no new warnings in touched code). - `cargo test --release -p graph --lib` (497 passed). - Flow suites, all pass: `test_multi_exec`, `test_bulk_insertion`, `test_concurrent_query`, `test_constraint`, `test_multi_writer`, `test_pause_replication_race`, `test_effects_commit`, `test_replication`. - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py` (145 passed). Not hot-path: a queued write makes the same single `new_version()` as before. Only the CAS moves, from the start of the query to escalation. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #3093, where an inline write (e.g., inside MULTI/EXEC) failed with "another write is in progress" and lost its changes when it ran while a queued write was still matching. A queued write now builds into an unclaimed fork and claims the MVCC write slot only when it escalates under the write lock, so an inline writer never finds the slot taken. If an inline writer commits during matching, the queued write discards its fork and re-runs from the start. **Behavior** - GRAPH.RECORD returns a retryable error on a stale fork instead of retrying. - The write slot is only held by threads that hold the write lock. Written for commit ad2925117a40fdb47325867c5e9238c0d4feb0e0. Summary will update on new commits.

title: fix: CowBTree rejects DOC_BYTES widths it cannot read back
body: Closes #3238 ## Problem `CowBTree`'s const assert accepted `DOC_BYTES ∈ 1..=8`, but the doc field is read back with `read_width`, which loads only 1/2/4/8 bytes and treats any other width as 8. `CowBTree::<256, 256, 3>` compiled and panicked on its second insert. Latent: the only production instantiation (numeric index) uses `DOC_BYTES = 8`. Different from the two CowBTree bugs in #2893 / #2897; found by the Lean model of #2278 (`LeafAosD.docBytes3_*`). ## Fix The smaller of the two options in the issue: a `const fn is_read_width(width) -> bool { matches!(width, 1 | 2 | 4 | 8) }` next to `read_width`, used by the three const asserts (`Default`, `new`, `from_sorted`), so the accepted set is defined by the reader. Supporting 3/5/6/7 would need a variable-length load in the hot read path for no current user. Compile-time only; no runtime code changes. | `CowBTree::<256, 256, 3>::new()` then two `insert`s | Result | |---|---| | Rust before | compiles; 2nd insert panics — debug: `assertion left == right failed` (`mod.rs:98`); release: `range end index 16 out of range for slice of length 11` (`mod.rs:99`) | | Rust after | compile error: `DOC_BYTES must be 1, 2, 4 or 8: it is the AoS doc field width, read back with read_width, which loads only those widths` | | C | n/a (no equivalent structure) | ## Tests - `doc_bytes_accepts_exactly_the_readable_widths`: `is_read_width` over `0..=16` accepts exactly `[1, 2, 4, 8]`, and `read_width` round-trips each accepted width. (On main the gate was inline `1..=8` and would have accepted 3/5/6/7; the old repro above panicked at runtime on main @ b033aecc6 and is a compile error after.) - `cargo test -p graph --lib cow_btree` 34 passed; `cargo test -p graph --lib` 496 passed, 1 failed (pre-existing `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, #2922). fmt / clippy clean; release build OK. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes `CowBTree` so `DOC_BYTES` values its reader cannot load are rejected at compile time instead of panicking at runtime. - The const assert previously accepted `DOC_BYTES ∈ 1..=8`, but `read_width` only loads 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes, so `CowBTree::<256, 256, 3>` compiled and panicked on its second insert. - Gates `DOC_BYTES` with the new `is_read_width` const fn, so widths 3/5/6/7 now fail to compile with a clear message. **Tests** - Adds a test verifying `is_read_width` accepts exactly `[1, 2, 4, 8]` and that each accepted width round-trips through `read_width`. - `cargo test -p graph --lib cow_btree` passes 34 tests; the full `graph` lib suite has one pre-existing failure unrelated to this change (#2922). Written for commit 3624880ed9acad54d578b2ead3321f5cd8960b84. Summary will update on new commits.

title: fix: a deleted edge no longer keeps its type after a constraint registers a new type
body: Closes #3244 ## Problem `Graph::get_type_id_mut` registered a relationship type and its tensor but did not call `resize()`, so `relationship_type_matrix` (edges x types) stayed one column short. `get_relationship_matrix_mut` and `get_label_id_mut` both resize for this reason. Its callers that register a type with no edge are `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE ... RELATIONSHIP ` on the primary and `ADD_SCHEMA` in effects apply on a replica. After that, edge deletes (`delete_relationships`, `delete_implicit_edges`) built a removal mask `relationship_cap x relationship_types.len()` that the narrower matrix refused with `GrB_DIMENSION_MISMATCH`. Only a `debug_assert` checks it, so in release the deleted edge kept its type, and the edge that reused its id read back with the old type. ## Fix Call `self.resize()` in `get_type_id_mut` after registering the type. `resize` costs a few comparisons when nothing changed, and this runs once per type ever. The one change covers both the primary and the replica path. ``` CREATE (:N)-[:A]->(:N) GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE g MANDATORY RELATIONSHIP B PROPERTIES 1 x MATCH ()-[r]->() DELETE r MATCH (a), (b) WHERE id(a) = 0 AND id(b) = 1 CREATE (a)-[:C]->(b) MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN id(r), type(r) ``` | | Rust before | Rust after | C | |---|---|---|---| | primary `type(r)` | `A` | `C` | `C` | | replica `type(r)` | `A` | `C` | n/a (C cannot read v3 effects) | ## Tests - New flow test `test_effects_ddl.py:testEffects_01_ConstraintAsEffect.test04_a_type_registered_by_a_constraint_does_not_stick_to_deleted_edges` runs the repro on a primary/replica pair and checks `type(r)` and the `:A` count on both sides. - Before the fix: fails twice, `[[0, 'A']] == [[0, 'C']]`, once for the primary and once for the replica. - After: passes. - Flow suites (release): `test_constraint.py` 26/26, `test_effects_topology.py` 3/3, `test_effects_opcodes.py` 12/12, `test_effects_ddl.py` 18/19. The one failure is `testEffects_06_ConstraintSettlingRaces.test02` (`[[1]] == [[2]]`). It also fails on `main` with the class run alone, and the test's own comment records it as a known intermittent failure. - `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. - `cargo test -p graph --lib`: all pass except the known macOS `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (#2922). `cargo fmt --check` is clean, with no clippy warnings in the touched code. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #3244: a deleted edge no longer keeps its type after a constraint registers a new type. `get_type_id_mut` registered a relationship type and its tensor but didn't resize `relationship_type_matrix`, so a type registered with no edge (a `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT` on the primary, an `ADD_SCHEMA` on a replica) left the edge×type matrix one column short. The next edge delete then built a removal mask the narrower matrix rejected — only a `debug_assert` caught the mismatch — so in release builds the deleted edge kept its type and the edge that reused its id read back the old type. The fix routes every type registration through `register_relationship_type`, a single helper that pushes the type name, inserts its tensor, and always calls `resize()`. Both `get_type_id_mut` and `get_relationship_matrix_mut` now go through it, so no registration site can skip the resize. `resize` costs a few comparisons when nothing changed and runs once per type. The change covers the primary and replica paths, and the new flow test runs the repro against both. Written for commit 5733f785611bbb41133ce8aa290be7fa9cd497e8. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Relationship types remain consistent across graph updates and constraints, including on replicas. When a deleted edge’s ID is reused for a different relationship type, the edge is associated only with its current type; stale associations are no longer retained on the master or replicas. This keeps relationship information accurate after edge changes.

title: fix: give graphs loaded from an RDB the configured CACHE_SIZE
body: Closes #3251 ## Problem `src/redis_type.rs` hard-coded `DEFAULT_CACHE_SIZE = 25` and passed it to `rdb_load_graph` in `graph_rdb_load` and `graphmeta_rdb_load`, and to the multi-key placeholder graph. So a graph loaded from an RDB (restart, `DEBUG RELOAD`, a replica's full sync) always had a 25-entry plan cache, whatever `CACHE_SIZE` the module was loaded with. Graphs created at run-time honour it. ## Fix The load callbacks run on the main thread, so `io_cache_size` takes the context Redis attaches to the IO handle (`RedisModule_GetContextFromIO`) and reads `CONFIGURATION_CACHE_SIZE` with it, the way `create_virtual_keys` already reads `VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT`. The constant is gone. `CACHE_SIZE 1`, `DEBUG RELOAD`, then `RETURN 1`, `RETURN 2`, `RETURN 1`: | | `main` | This PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | `Cached execution` | 0, 0, **1** | 0, 0, 0 | 0, 0, 0 | ## Tests - New flow test `test_cache.testCache.test_15_cache_size_survives_rdb_load` (`CACHE_SIZE 1`, reload, check a second query evicts the first). - Before: `True == False` FAIL at the last `RETURN 1`. - After: pass. - Flow (RLTest, release): `test_cache` 15/15, `test_encode_decode` 19/19 (multi-key load path, `VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT 10`), `test_persistency` 11/11, `test_rdb_load` 2/2, `test_replication` 2/2. - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. `cargo fmt --check` clean; `clippy --all-targets` has no warnings in touched code. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes graphs loaded from an RDB (restart, `DEBUG RELOAD`, or replica full sync) so they use the configured `CACHE_SIZE` instead of the previously hard-coded default of 25. Load callbacks run on the main thread, so they now read the configured value through the context Redis attaches to the IO handle, matching how graphs created at runtime behave. - Adds a flow test that reloads with `CACHE_SIZE 1` and verifies a second query evicts the first from the cache. - Closes #3251. Written for commit 52e5fe159bf3391b98ad7e4754dc6adb16c539ad. Summary will update on new commits.

title: fix: reload an index on an attribute named `range:x` under that name
body: Closes #3239 ## Problem Since #2459 the RDB encoder writes each index field's bare attribute name, as C does. The decoder (`decode_index_field`, `src/serializers/mod.rs`) still stripped a `range:` / `vector:` prefix from the name it read, a leftover from before that change. An attribute literally called `range:x` (or `vector:v`) therefore came back after `DEBUG RELOAD` / restart as an index on `x`, and the index stopped serving `n.`range:x``. All released Rust versions (6.0.0+) already write bare names, so no released RDB carries a prefix. ## Fix Use the name as read. The prefixed RediSearch field name is still built by `create_index_sync` when the index is rebuilt. | After `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.`range:x`)` + `DEBUG RELOAD` | `main` | This PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | `db.indexes()` properties | `[x]` | `[range:x]` | `[range:x]` | | `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.`range:x` = 1` plan | Label Scan + Filter | Index Scan | Index Scan | ## Tests - New flow test `test_encode_decode.test_19_index_on_attribute_named_like_a_field_prefix` (range index on `range:x`, vector index on `vector:v`, reload, check names and that the index still serves the query). - Before: `['v', 'x'] == ['range:x', 'vector:v']` FAIL, and `'Aggregate / Filter / Node By Label Scan' should contain 'Index Scan'` FAIL. - After: pass. - Flow (RLTest, release): `test_encode_decode` 20/20, `test_rdb_load` 2/2, `test_index_create` 18/18, `test_vecsim` 12/12, `test_constraint` 26/26, `test_graph_copy` 9/9, `test_persistency` 11/11. - `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py`: 131 passed. `cargo fmt --check` clean; `clippy --all-targets` has no warnings in touched code. ## Release note RDBs written by pre-6.0 development builds of the Rust engine (before #2459) stored index fields under their RediSearch names (`range:age`). They now load with the index on an attribute of that literal name, which is left unused; re-create those range/vector indexes. Every 6.0.x release, and C, write the bare attribute name and are unaffected. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes RDB reload so an index on an attribute literally named `range:x` or `vector:v` comes back under that name. The decoder in `src/serializers/mod.rs` still stripped `range:`/`vector:` prefixes that the encoder stopped writing in #2459, so such an attribute came back as an index on `x` and stopped serving queries. **Bug Fixes** - Read the index field name verbatim; the prefixed RediSearch field name is still built when the index is rebuilt. - Adds a flow test covering range and vector indexes on prefixed attribute names after `DEBUG RELOAD`, checking the name and that the index still serves the query. Written for commit a9f12a0d95a3e070ab36e54771f6802335db30f8. title: fix: slow log no longer panics on a multi-byte character at byte 2048
body: Closes #3233 ## Problem The slow log sliced the query and parameter text at byte 2048 (`entry_hash` and `truncate` in `src/slow_log.rs`). Slicing a `&str` inside a multi-byte character panics, so a query (or `CYPHER` parameter string) longer than 2048 bytes that ran past the 10 ms threshold, with a character straddling byte 2048, killed the server: ``` FalkorDB panic: panicked at src/slow_log.rs:49:10: end byte index 2048 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 2047..2049 of string) ``` ## Fix A `prefix` helper returns the longest prefix of at most 2048 bytes that ends on a char boundary (`str::floor_char_boundary`, already used in the lexer). `entry_hash` hashes that prefix and `truncate` stores it plus `...`. Nothing else in `src/` slices text by a byte limit unsafely: `telemetry.rs` cuts by `char_indices`, `divergence_guard.rs::clip` walks to a boundary, and the `graph_core.rs` slices are at NUL / params offsets. Query: 2050 bytes, `é` at bytes 2047..2049, `UNWIND range(1, 2000000) …` so it is logged. | | `main` | This PR | C | |---|---|---|---| | query answers | no, server panics and exits | yes | yes | | `GRAPH.SLOWLOG` query text | — | 2047 bytes + `...` (2050 bytes, valid UTF-8) | 2048 bytes + `...` (2051 bytes, ends `\xc3...`: half of `é`, invalid UTF-8) | | same with the character in a `CYPHER p='…'` prefix | panics at `slow_log.rs:32` | params 2047 bytes + `...` | 2048 bytes + `...`, invalid UTF-8 | The stored text differs from C only where C stores a broken character; we drop the whole character (up to 3 bytes fewer) and keep the reply valid UTF-8. Matching C byte for byte would mean storing and returning non-UTF-8 bytes. Unchanged: C also appends `...` to text that is exactly 2048 bytes long, which Rust did not do before and still does not. ## Tests - New flow test `test_slowlog.py::test07_truncate_on_char_boundary`: for `é`, `€` and `😀` straddling byte 2048, in the query text and in the parameters, it checks the server answers and `GRAPH.SLOWLOG` holds both entries, cut before the character. - Before the fix (release build of `main`): fails, `Connection closed by server`, the server process is gone. - After: passes; `test_slowlog.py` 7/7. - No Rust unit test: the `falkordb-rs` crate's test binary aborts at start (`the Redis Allocator isn't available`), since the module's global allocator is Redis's, so `src/` has no runnable unit tests. - `cargo fmt --check` clean, no clippy warnings in `slow_log.rs`, `cargo test -p graph --lib` 495 passed (only the known #2922 failure), `pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py` 131 passed. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes a server panic when the slow log truncated a query or `CYPHER` parameter string longer than 2048 bytes whose multi-byte character straddled byte 2048; slicing the `&str` at that byte panicked and took down the server. Truncation and the dedup hash now cut at the nearest character boundary at or below 2048 bytes via `str::floor_char_boundary`, so the whole character is dropped and stored text stays valid UTF-8. This differs from C only where C stores a broken character; otherwise behavior matches, including not appending `...` to text that is exactly 2048 bytes. Adds a flow test covering `é`, `€`, and `😀` straddling byte 2048 in both the query text and the parameters. Closes #3233. Written for commit be7a3ae20320f44c8025faad721a2cb1c84920da. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Slow-log entries now truncate long query text and CYPHER parameter values at valid character boundaries, preventing multibyte characters from being split or corrupted. * Truncated values end with an ellipsis. Long queries containing multibyte characters are also handled safely when generating query hashes.

title: ci(backport): read every search result in batch-backport
body: Closes #3191. The batch-backport workflow now reads every PR its search matches, not only the first 30. - **Paging:** the search asks for 100 results per page and reads every page (`gh api --paginate --slurp`). Results are sorted by creation time instead of last update, so a PR can't move between pages while they are read. - **Count check:** the run stops with an error if the number of PRs read differs from the search's `total_count`. - **Search start:** the search starts at the tag's full UTC timestamp instead of its day, so PRs merged later on the tag's day are included. --- ## Summary by cubic The batch-backport workflow now backports every PR its search matches instead of only the first 30. - Pages through all search results (100 per page) sorted by creation time, so a PR can't shift between pages while they're fetched. - Fails with an error if the number of PRs read doesn't match the search's `total_count`, preventing partial backports. - Starts the search at the tag's full UTC timestamp rather than its day, so PRs merged later on the tag's day are included. Written for commit 10060413f4c3450f9d2ef5e18a15f7371e83868b. title: build(docker): run redis-server as the falkordb user
body: Closes #3180 Runs `redis-server` in the Docker image as the unprivileged `falkordb` user instead of root, following the official redis image's entrypoint. ### `build/runtime/run.sh` The container starts as root, as before. When it is root, has `CAP_SETUID` and `CAP_SETGID`, and `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS` is unset, `run.sh`: 1. hands the data directory to `falkordb` (`chown` of whatever it does not already own), but only when the directory holds nothing except `*.rdb`, `nodes*.conf` and `appendonlydir`, and prints a notice otherwise; 2. after `gen-certs.sh` (with `TLS=1`), hands `falkordb` the certificate and key files that script generates, and only those; 3. sets `umask 0077` when the umask is the default `0022`; 4. execs `redis-server` through `gosu falkordb`, so `redis-server` stays PID 1. `SKIP_FIX_PERMS=1` skips steps 1 and 2. Started with `--user`, without those capabilities, or with `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1`, it runs `redis-server` as the current user. The variable names and the data-directory check follow the official image; `nodes*.conf` is added for cluster nodes. The browser still starts first and drops to `nextjs` through its own entrypoint. ### `build/runtime/Dockerfile` - creates `falkordb` (uid/gid 999) in place of the `redis` account at the same ids; - installs `gosu` in the `server` stage (the `full` stage installed it for the browser; it now inherits it); - owns `/var/lib/falkordb/data` and `/var/lib/falkordb/tls` as `root:falkordb`, mode 0775, so `falkordb` writes through the group and root remains the owner. ### CI images and test harness - `Dockerfile.asan` and `Dockerfile.coverage` set `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1`; the coverage image's account is renamed to `falkordb` to match. - `tests/flow/common.py` sets mode 0777 on the `--logfile` directory and on `mountable_mkdtemp()` directories it creates for spawned containers, so `redis-server` can use them as `falkordb`. --- ## Summary by cubic Runs redis-server in the Docker image as the unprivileged `falkordb` user (uid/gid 999) instead of root, matching the official redis image's entrypoint. Closes #3180. The container still starts as root: run.sh hands the data directory and the TLS files gen-certs.sh generates to `falkordb`, then execs redis-server through gosu so it stays PID 1. It stays root when started with `--user`, without CAP_SETUID/CAP_SETGID, or with `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1`; `SKIP_FIX_PERMS=1` skips the ownership steps. The data directory is re-owned only when it holds nothing but `*.rdb`, `nodes*.conf` and `appendonlydir`; anything else prints a notice and is left alone. If any handover chown fails, redis-server also stays root. New files are created with `umask 0077`. The `redis` account at uid/gid 999 is now `falkordb`; `gosu` moves to the server stage, and the data and TLS directories are `root:falkordb` mode 0775. The ASAN and coverage images set `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1` and the coverage account is renamed to match. The flow-test harness makes its log and temp directories writable by `falkordb`. Written for commit fc239e8cde959463a5c40a81f9884927ed1a29ab. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Runtime** * Runtime containers now use a dedicated service account instead of the Redis account. * When supported, the server drops root privileges before starting and adjusts permissions for recognized data and TLS files. If the data directory contains unrecognized files or ownership cannot be changed, Redis continues running as root. * Permission changes can be skipped. Runtime variants without the required account or tools continue to run without privilege dropping. * Runtime data and TLS directories have updated ownership and access permissions. * **Bug Fixes** * CI-created temporary and log directories now have permissions that allow mounted workflows to access them.

title: ci: port master's Trivy image scan; drop util-linux from the runtime image
body:
Closes #3178

Ports master's Trivy image gate (`security-scan` in `build.yml`) to the Rust pipeline, which had no image scan, and removes `util-linux` from the runtime image, which clears 32 of the 36 unfixed HIGH Debian findings in `:edge`.

### What it does

New `security-scan` job in `_ci-pipeline.yml`, after `build-rc-image`, image vehicle only:

- scans `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb:rc-<ci_key>-{x64,arm64v8}` (`full` is `FROM server`, so it covers both repos);
- fails on HIGH/CRITICAL with a fixed version (`ignore-unfixed`), same rule as master;
- uploads the full JSON report as `trivy-report-<arch>` (30 days);
- lists blocking findings in the run summary. Master posts a PR comment instead, which needs `pull-requests: write` and has nowhere to go in the merge queue.

Pins match master: trivy-action `ed142fd…` (verified as upstream `v0.36.0`), Trivy `v0.69.2`. A failure fails `ci-pipeline`, which `ci-gate` already requires.

The queue scans `rc-mg-<sha>`, which is what `:edge` and releases retag, so the gate covers what ships. Fork PRs build no image and skip the job; their queue entry is scanned.

### Trivy gate: verified locally (Trivy v0.69.2, same flags)

| Image | Result |
|---|---|
| `falkordb/falkordb:edge` (built 2026-10-07), amd64 + arm64 | passes: 0 blocking (36 HIGH Debian, none fixable) |
| `falkordb/falkordb:v4.0.7` | fails: 1,433 blocking (run with `--exit-code 3` to rule out an error exit) |
| `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb:rc-pr-2908-{x64,arm64v8}`, no `--image-src` | both arches resolve from the registry; 10 blocking (image built 2026-09-24) |

The summary's `jq` filter selects the same 1,433 findings as the gate on `v4.0.7`. `actionlint` is clean on the changed file. This PR's own CI is the first real run of the job.

### Runtime image: drop util-linux, mount, bsdutils

`build/runtime/Dockerfile` (server stage) now force-purges `util-linux`, `mount`, `bsdutils` and their libraries (`libmount1`, `libblkid1`, `libuuid1`, `libsmartcols1`, `liblastlog2-2`), next to the existing ncurses/perl/login/passwd trim.

`:edge` has 36 HIGH Debian findings, all `affected` (Debian has no fixed package yet). They are 7 CVEs counted once per binary package, and 4 util-linux CVEs across those 8 packages make up 32 of them: privilege escalation through the setuid `mount`/`umount`/`su` and `nsenter`. Nothing in the image uses them. `run.sh`, `gen-certs.sh` and the browser's `docker-entrypoint.sh` call none of their commands, and `apt-cache rdepends --installed` finds no other installed package that depends on the eight.

This purge has no `|| true`. If a dependent ever appears, the build fails instead of silently keeping the packages, which the gate would not flag because it ignores unfixed findings.

Verified on arm64 by building the real Dockerfile's `full` target with only `builder` and `redis-builder` swapped for `:edge`'s binaries (`--build-context`):

| Check | `:edge` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Image build, incl. server-stage sanity RUN and `full` stage's `apt-get install` after the purge | — | passes |
| `GRAPH.QUERY` (create + aggregate) | ok | identical result |
| Browser on :3000 | 200 | 200 |
| `TLS=1` (`gen-certs.sh`, query over TLS) | — | ok |

title: fix(rdb): save virtual keys as graphmeta so C keeps graphs in GRAPH.LIST
body: Fixes the `GRAPH.LIST` part of #3160. ## Problem When a graph is large enough to be saved across several RDB keys (more than `VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT` entities, 100k by default), Rust saved the extra "virtual" keys with the `graphdata` type. C uses `graphmeta` for these keys. When C 4.20.x loads such an RDB: 1. It loads each `graphdata` virtual key as a graph and adds the graph to its list of graphs. 2. When loading ends, it deletes the virtual keys. 3. Deleting a `graphdata` key runs `_GraphContextType_Free`, which calls `Globals_RemoveGraph(gc)`. That removes the shared graph from the list `GRAPH.LIST` reads. As a result, after a downgrade the graph is still queryable but missing from `GRAPH.LIST`. C also removes graphs from that list while iterating over it, so other graphs' virtual keys were skipped and stayed in the keyspace. ## Fix - Rust now saves virtual keys as `graphmeta`, the type C uses. The key holds only the dummy value `graphmeta_free` already expects. - `graphmeta_rdb_save` now writes the key's slice of the graph, using a `save_key_slice` helper shared with `graph_rdb_save`. - Rust already loads `graphmeta` keys through the C-RDB load path, so loading C RDBs or Rust's own RDBs is unchanged. RDBs from 6.0.x (with `graphdata` virtual keys) still load as before. - Removed the comments claiming C can't load `graphmeta`. ## Verification Rust-saved RDB loaded by C (local macOS C build, `VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT 10`, two graphs with deleted nodes and edges): | | `GRAPH.LIST` on C | leftover virtual keys | ids / counts | |---|---|---|---| | before | *(empty)* | 5 keys of graph `b` | preserved | | after | `a b` | none | preserved | The same before-result reproduces with the published images (`falkordb/falkordb:6.0.1` → `:v4.20.7`). Also checked: - C → fixed Rust → fixed Rust: `GRAPH.LIST`, node ids and counts preserved, no leftover keys. - Flow tests: `test_rdb_load` now asserts that virtual keys are typed `graphmeta`. It fails on the pre-fix module and passes with the fix. `test_encode_decode` (19 tests) and `test_graph_copy` (9 tests) pass. ## Not covered The issue also reports node ids changing after the downgrade. I couldn't reproduce that with deleted node/edge ids, range and vector indexes, a 150k-node graph, deleted-id lists split across 6 virtual keys, or C save/reload cycles after the downgrade. I've left it open on the issue. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes graphs vanishing from `GRAPH.LIST` after a C FalkorDB downgrade loads an RDB saved by Rust. When a graph spans multiple RDB keys, Rust saved the virtual keys as `graphdata`. C loads each as a graph, then deletes them, and its free callback removes the shared graph from the list `GRAPH.LIST` reads, making the graph disappear from the list while staying queryable. Rust now types virtual keys `graphmeta`, matching C. `graphmeta_rdb_save` writes each key's slice via a `save_key_slice` helper also used by `graph_rdb_save`. Loading is unchanged: Rust already reads `graphmeta` keys, and RDBs from 6.0.x with `graphdata` virtual keys still load as before. Written for commit abd835bd0490793535ccbb578f59154d3aa0162d. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * RDB saves now preserve assigned slices for graph keys and virtual keys. When a slice cannot be applied, the graph is saved directly instead. * Virtual keys created during saves use the `graphmeta` Redis type, and restored virtual keys are checked to retain that type. * Virtual keys without an assigned slice are not written to the RDB file.

title: ci(images): rebuild the OS-package stages on every image build
body:
Closes #3152

## Problem

The runtime image build restores a registry buildcache (`_build-flavour.yml`). Docker keys a cached `RUN` on its command text and parent layer, not on what the Debian archive holds. So when the `server` stage hits the cache, `apt-get upgrade` never runs and the image ships packages as old as the cache entry. A security update Debian publishes between two rebuilds of the `debian:trixie-slim` base is silently skipped.

This is what an external scan of `6.0.0` is asking for: it ships OpenSSL `3.5.7-1~deb13u2`, and Debian's `deb13u3` fixes the five reported CVEs.

## Change

On the build step in `_build-flavour.yml`:

```yaml
pull: true
no-cache-filters: |
  server
  full
```

- The `server` and `full` stages, the ones that install OS packages, are never served from the cache.
- The compile stages (`builder`, `redis-builder`) stay cached. `redis-server` and `falkordb.so` link `libssl`/`libcrypto`/`libz` dynamically (checked with `ldd`), so the versions that ship come from `server`.
- `full` is `FROM server` and already reruns with it; it is named so that does not depend on it.
- `Dockerfile.asan` has no `full` stage; a filter naming a stage that doesn't exist is ignored, not an error.

## Verification

Checked on the real `build/runtime/Dockerfile` with a fresh `docker-container` builder on `moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1`, the image `setup-buildx-action` uses. The `builder` stage was swapped for the released `falkordb.so` via `--build-context` so nothing had to be compiled; `redis-builder`, `server` and `full` were built for real.

1. Seeded a local cache (`--cache-to type=local,mode=max`).
2. Cleared the builder's own state, then rebuilt from that cache two ways:

| Step | Current config | With this change |
|---|---|---|
| `[server 2/12]` apt install + `apt-get upgrade` | CACHED | ran (15.3 s) |
| `[full 1/5]` apt install | CACHED | ran (2.8 s) |
| `[redis-builder 6/6]` redis compile | CACHED | CACHED |

The image built with the change has `openssl`, `libssl3t64` and `openssl-provider-legacy` at `3.5.7-1~deb13u3`. A filter naming a missing stage exits 0 on the same builder.

CI can't show the difference on this PR. The buildcache was last written on 2026-09-17, before the current Debian base, so today every runtime build already reruns these steps (0 cached steps in merge-queue run 36303922883).

## Build time

None today, for the reason above. When the cache does hit, this adds the cost of the two stages: in run 36303922883, the `server` apt step took 12.7–15.7 s, the `full` apt step 2.6 s, and every other step in those stages under 1 s. They also run in parallel with the engine compile.

## Not in this PR

- Already-published images are untouched; releases retag the merge-queue image rather than building. `6.0` needs a patch release (6.0.1) to pick up the fix, plus a backport of this change.
- The buildcache stopped being written when #2718 moved image builds into the merge queue, because `cache-to` is gated on `refs/heads/main`. Whether to revive it is a separate, performance-only decision.

title: Handle short reads gracefully during RDB decode
body:
Closes #3140

Also fixes the C side of #2506 (the Rust side is #2510).

## Problem

A truncated RDB payload (a diskless replication stream that drops mid-transfer, a truncated `RESTORE`/`MIGRATE` payload, a cut-off `dump.rdb`) crashed the server: FalkorDB never declared `REDISMODULE_OPTIONS_HANDLE_IO_ERRORS`, so Redis panicked on the first short read.

Malformed but checksum-valid payloads either crashed the server (`RedisModule_Assert`, and libc `assert`, which release builds keep on) or, where the check was a debug-only `ASSERT`, loaded silently in release builds.

## Changes

**Short reads**
- `module.c`: declare `REDISMODULE_OPTIONS_HANDLE_IO_ERRORS`.
- `SerializerIO`: a sticky error flag. Once a read fails, every later read returns zero or an empty buffer without touching the stream, and the decoders stop at their next checkpoint.
- v19 and v20 decoders: checkpoints in every loop. On failure the decoder returns NULL and frees the partial graph unless an earlier virtual key already registered it (`RdbLoadGraph`, `Decode_Previous`).
- Both graph key types (`graphdata` and the `graphmeta` virtual keys) hand NULL back to Redis instead of registering it.

**Malformed payloads** (v19, v20, and the buffered reader they share)
- `SerializerIO_SetError(io, reason)` fails the decode through the same flag. Converted to failures:
  - buffer framing and value type tags (these crashed release builds);
  - count and consistency checks that were debug-only `ASSERT`s;
  - GraphBLAS load results;
  - duplicate or out-of-order schemas and duplicate constraints;
  - out-of-range entity, label and constraint ids;
  - index language, field type and vector metric.
- One warning per rejected key, naming the key and the reason:
  `Failed loading graph key '<key>': <reason>`
  Short reads add no line of ours; Redis reports those itself.

**UDFs**
- Libraries in the RDB load with replace. Loading an RDB into a process that already holds a library (a replica's next full sync, `DEBUG RELOAD`) now leaves the RDB's version in place. Before, debug builds asserted and release builds kept the stale copy.
- A library that fails to load fails the load.

**RESTORE over a live graph of the same name** (fixes the C side of #2506)
- The decoder found the graph to extend by the name stored in the payload. That lookup is meant for graphs split across keys, but it matched any registered graph, live ones included.
- `RESTORE` decodes before deleting the value it replaces. So `RESTORE … REPLACE` of a graph's own dump, or a `RESTORE` under another key while the source is live, decoded into the live graph: its contents doubled, and with an index the server crashed in `Index_SetLanguage`.
- Now only a graph part-way through a multi-key load is extended. Otherwise the payload decodes into a new graph, and Redis frees the replaced one as usual.

**Merge with master (v20)**
- master moved the v19 decoder to `decoders/prev/v19` and added `decoders/current/v20`. The hardening is applied to both.
- `Decode_Previous` no longer frees the v19 serializer before checking it for an error.
- `CCHIndex_RdbLoad` returns NULL on a short read.

## Behavior changes

- `RESTORE … REPLACE` of a graph's own dump now restores exactly the dump. Before, it doubled the graph, and crashed when the graph had an index.

- Release builds now refuse payloads that broke a debug-only check and used to load silently:
  - `RESTORE` fails with `Bad data format`;
  - at startup, Redis exits;
  - on a replica's full sync, the replica exits.
- Replicas configured with `repl-diskless-load on-empty-db` now actually load from the socket. Before, Redis skipped diskless loading because a module didn't declare IO-error handling.
  - A dropped connection makes the replica retry.
  - Rejected data makes the replica exit, which is Redis's policy for corrupt data.

## Scope

- Covered: the v19 and v20 decoders, and the buffered reader they share.
- v14–v18: their decoders are unchanged, including the graph lookup by name. They pick up the short-read latch from the shared reader.
- v10–v13: read Redis's IO directly; unchanged.
- Out of scope:
  - `GRAPH.RESTORE` / `GRAPH.COPY`;
  - allocations sized from header counts;
  - GraphBLAS matrix contents.

## Tests

- `test_rdb_load.py`:
  - a short read inside every chunk of a multi-chunk graph;
  - a short read inside a `graphmeta` key;
  - a malformed type tag, buffer length and payload type;
  - `DEBUG RELOAD` replacing a UDF library;
  - `RESTORE … REPLACE` of a graph's own dump, with and without an index (the #2506 reproducer);
  - `RESTORE` under another key while the source graph is live.

  Each new test fails on the code before its fix; the multi-chunk short-read test on debug builds, where the assert it trips lives.
- Run locally (linux arm64, release and debug builds):
  - truncation inside every chunk of a 25 MB graph: all rejected cleanly, memory flat;
  - diskless replication with the stream cut at 17 points: all recover;
  - 400 seeded single-byte corruptions of a valid DUMP:

    | | Crashes before | Crashes after |
    |---|---|---|
    | Release | 134 (+5 hangs) | 3 |
    | Debug | 141 (+1 hang) | 4 (+1 hang) |

    The remaining crashes are GraphBLAS matrix contents and oversized header counts, both out of scope.

title: Fix crash when a clause errors mid plan-build (#250)
body:
Resolve: #3138
A build-time error raised while constructing a clause left plan construction in a poisoned state: the clause / segment loops never checked ErrorCtx_EncounteredError(), so subsequent clauses (a segment boundary WITH, an OPTIONAL MATCH, ORDER BY, UNWIND, a CALL {} subquery, ...) were still built on top of a partially-constructed / NULL-rooted plan. The malformed plan then crashed the server when the segments were tied together (_tie_segments) or when the plan was freed (OpBase_Free -> HashTableRelease, the reported signature).

This is the general form of the MERGE-only fix in #239/#3116: the reported query is a read query whose erroring clause precedes an OPTIONAL MATCH.

Fixes:
- stop building once a clause raises an error (ExecutionPlan_Populate- ExecutionPlan) and once a segment raises an error (_process_segments)
- in ExecutionPlan_FromTLS_AST, tear down the partial segments and return NULL instead of tying / adding an implicit result to a broken plan
- guard buildCallSubqueryPlan against a NULL / errored embedded plan before dereferencing it (mirrors the buildMergeOp guard), matching the new NULL-on-error contract of ExecutionPlan_FromTLS_AST

Regression tests added to test_optional_match.py (test28, the reported read-query shape) and test_call_subquery.py (test_54). Both trigger the error during plan construction via a non-boolean WHERE predicate (which passes AST validation), and were verified to crash the server without the fix.

title: fix(runtime): allow startNode() and endNode() to accept null (#2723)
body:
Closes #2723.

## Problem
In the Rust query engine, passing `null` to `startNode()` or `endNode()` (such as when evaluating expressions over unmatched `OPTIONAL MATCH` patterns or literal scalar calls) failed with a runtime type mismatch error:
```
Type mismatch: expected Edge but was Null
```

Per the FalkorDB documentation and openCypher specification, `startNode(null)` and `endNode(null)` must return `null` (three-valued logic / null propagation). The C engine (`v4.20.4`) already returns `null` correctly.

## Root Cause
In `graph/src/runtime/functions/entity.rs`, `startnode` and `endnode` were registered with:
```rust
args: [Type::Relationship]
```

title: fix(functions): name received types in the engine's vocabulary in entity.rs
body:
Closes #3126

﻿Four type-mismatch messages in `entity.rs` that are not written in the engine's own type vocabulary. Both are one-liners; this is a message-correctness fix, not a behaviour change.

## 1. `indegree`/`outdegree` use Rust's `Debug` spelling

`parse_degree_args` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/entity.rs:304`) hand-rolls its type check because `indegree`/`outdegree` are registered `var_arg: Type::Any` → `FnArguments::VarLength`, and both `GraphFn::validate` and `validate_args_type` are deliberate no-ops for var-len. So that check is the **only** one these functions get, and its message is the user-facing one. All three sites formatted the received type with `{:?}`.

`Type` derives `Debug` **and** has a hand-written `Display` impl at `mod.rs:610-654` whose entire purpose is the user-facing vocabulary (`Self::Int => "Integer"`, `Self::Bool => "Boolean"`, `Self::Relationship => "Edge"`). The framework's own message uses `{}` (`mod.rs:836-842`), and C uses `SIType_ToString`, which returns `"Integer"`.

| query | before | after / C |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN indegree(1)` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `RETURN outdegree(n, [1])` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `RETURN outdegree(n, 'R', 1)` | `...but was Int` | `...but was Integer` |
| `RETURN outdegree(n, 'R', ['X'])` | `...but was List(List(Any))` | `...but was List` |

The last one is the worst: it leaks the internal `Type::List(Type::Any)` structure into a string a user reads. Three `{:?}` → `{}`.

## 2. `hasLabels` drops the received type on its catch-all

`has_labels` checks list element types by hand, and three arms name what arrived — `but was Integer`, `but was Float`, `but was Boolean`. The catch-all covers the other **12** `Value` variants and said nothing:

```
MATCH (n) WHERE hasLabels(n, ['person', null])   ->  Type mismatch: expected String
MATCH (n) WHERE hasLabels(n, ['person', {a:1}])  ->  Type mismatch: expected String
```

It was the only type-mismatch message in the file without a `but was X` clause. Now uses `Value::name()`, the same helper the rest of the codebase uses for this, and whose spellings match the three arms above it.

## Testing

**`cargo test -p graph`** — new `mod tests` in `entity.rs` (the file had none). `parse_degree_args` is a module-private pure function and every one of the three sites returns before a `Runtime` is touched, so no harness is needed:
- the four mismatch spellings above,
- `the_arity_message_is_untouched` — the "Received 3 arguments ... expected at most 2" path is a different branch and must not change,
- `the_accepted_shapes_are_untouched` — `degree(node)` and `degree(node, ['R'])` still parse.

**Flow suite** — new `test19a_hasLabels_type_mismatch_names_the_received_type` in `tests/flow/test_function_calls.py` (listed in `flow_tests_done.txt`), covering all six reachable element types. Written as `error = None` + `assertTrue(error is not None, ...)` rather than the try/except shape used by the neighbouring test, so it cannot pass vacuously if the query stops raising.

**No existing assertion moves.** `test_function_calls.py:2415`/`:2432` assert only the substrings `"Type mismatch"` / `"Received"`, and the existing `hasLabels` assertion at `:627` goes through the untouched `Value::Int` arm — and `Value::name()` returns `"Integer"` for it anyway. `Steps.py` in the TCK asserts only `"Type mismatch" in str(e)`.

## Relation to #340

#340 asks for *more* in these messages (function name, argument index). This is orthogonal — it makes the existing message well-formed rather than adding fields. Either can land first.
