title: ci(release): move Docker Hub :latest to the Rust image on release
body:
Closes #2881

## Problem
When a release is the highest semver, the retag job in `release-image.yml` tags GHCR `:latest`, but on Docker Hub it tags only `:latest-rs`. `release-tag.yml` takes this path on a `v6.*` tag push. So tagging `v6.0.0` would leave `docker.io/falkordb/{falkordb,falkordb-server}:latest` on the C v4.20.6 image.

## Change
- The retag path now also tags `falkordb/${REPO}:latest` on Docker Hub. That matches the rebuild path (`_build-flavour.yml`), which already moves bare `:latest` on both registries.
- `:latest-rs` is dropped. Bare `:latest` replaces it, and it was never published on Docker Hub (`docker.io/falkordb/falkordb:latest-rs` returns not found), so nothing is pinned to it.
- The `:latest` decision itself is unchanged. It still requires the release to be the highest non-draft, non-prerelease semver, so a backport patch on an old version branch doesn't move it.

## Not in this PR
C's `release-image.yml` on `4.20` and `master` sets `IS_LATEST=1` on every release event. That means the next C 4.20.x release would move Docker Hub `:latest` back to C. It needs its own fix on those branches.

## Backport
This goes to `6.0` through the merge queue before `v6.0.0` is tagged. That queue run also builds the `rc-mg-<sha>` image the release retag needs, which `f0f23ead` doesn't have.

## Verification
- `actionlint`: no new findings. The one SC2086 on the deliberately unquoted `$EXTRA_TAGS` is already on `main`.
- Not exercised end to end: this path only runs on a release.

title: fix: pattern comprehensions everywhere — no crashes, nested plans for loop variables (#2308)
body:
Closes #2308

## Problem

The planner turns a pattern comprehension into its own sub-plan only in `WHERE`, projections, `UNWIND` and `FOREACH`. Anywhere else, the comprehension reaches `unreachable!("PatternComprehension should be handled by the planner")` in `eval.rs` and panics the module, which takes the whole server down. The issue reports one position (inline relationship properties). A sweep on `main` found more, plus two positions that gave wrong results or errors rather than crashing:

| Position | Example | `main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inline properties: node, relationship, var-length, CREATE, MERGE | `MATCH ()-[{k:size([(a)-->()\|1])}]-() RETURN 1` | crash | error, same as C |
| `SET` (`=`, `+=`, map) | `MATCH (n) SET n.p = size([(n)-->() \| 1])` | crash | correct result |
| `DELETE` | `MATCH (n) DELETE [(n)-->(y) \| y][0]` | crash | correct result |
| `REMOVE` | `MATCH (n) REMOVE head([(n)-->(y) \| y]).k` | crash | correct result |
| `ORDER BY` | `RETURN n.name ORDER BY size([(n)<--() \| 1])` | `Variable ? not found` | correct result |
| Reads a list-comprehension / quantifier / `reduce` variable | `[x IN ns \| size([(x)-->() \| 1])]` | silently wrong (`[1,1]`) | correct result (`[1,0]`) |
| Procedure arguments | `CALL db.idx.fulltext.queryNodes('A', head([(n)-->(y) \| y.name]))` | crash | correct result |
| `YIELD … WHERE` | `CALL db.labels() YIELD label WHERE size([(a)-->() \| 1]) > 0` | crash | correct result |
| `LOAD CSV FROM` | `LOAD CSV FROM head([(f)-->(x) \| x.file]) AS row` | crash | correct result |
| `MERGE … ON CREATE / ON MATCH SET` | `MERGE (n:A) ON MATCH SET n.p = size([(n)-->() \| 1])` | crash | error (C errors too) |
| Index `OPTIONS` | `CREATE VECTOR INDEX … OPTIONS {dimension: size([(a)-->() \| 1]) + 1, …}` | crash | error |

C rejects every crashing shape above with an error, and errors on `ORDER BY` too. For the loop-variable row, C is silently wrong the same way when the variable is in the pattern, and errors when it isn't. This PR returns correct results wherever a sub-plan can run, and rejects the rest.

## Fix

- **SET item order.** A later SET item sees what earlier ones set, and consecutive `SET`s become one operator. So an item with a comprehension starts a new `Set`, fed by the `Set` holding the items before it: in `SET n.p = 1, n.q = head([(n)-->() | n.p])`, `q` is 1.
- **Clause expressions.** `SET`, `REMOVE`, `DELETE`, procedure arguments and `LOAD CSV` now move their comprehensions into an Apply chain below the operator. This is the same mechanism `UNWIND`/`FOREACH` already use, now shared as `extract_clause_expr_comprehensions`. `descend_clause_expr_applies` makes stitching put the preceding clause below that chain.
- **`YIELD … WHERE`** now uses the same WHERE planning as `MATCH` and `WITH`, factored out of both as `plan_filter`. So pattern predicates (`WHERE (node)-->()`, `NOT`, `OR`) work there too.
- **Parser rejections**, for the three places no sub-plan can run:
  - inline property maps;
  - MERGE's `ON CREATE`/`ON MATCH SET` (MERGE applies those itself after matching);
  - index `OPTIONS` (evaluated once, with no input row).

  While parsing those places, the parser holds a `ForbiddenPatternComprehension` (a thiserror enum) naming the place, and rejects a comprehension at the point it recognizes one. There's no walk over the tree afterwards. `parse_map` already passes `allow_pattern_predicate = false`, so bare pattern predicates were already refused there.

### Two pre-existing scope-table bugs

The planner mints fresh variables at `scope_vars[scope].len()`, and two cases fed it an incomplete table:

- **UNION branches** are bound by their own binders, whose tables were discarded. So a comprehension result overwrote a branch variable, giving e.g. `Type mismatch: expected Map … but was List`. This happens even with plain `RETURN`, no `SET` needed.
- **A `CALL {}` body's** scopes were popped with it. So a sub-plan inside a `CALL` that ends the query indexed past the table and panicked. This also happens with `UNWIND`/`WITH … WHERE` comprehensions.

The binder now keeps those retired tables and reports the largest one for each scope.

### Also

`db.idx.fulltext.drop(<non-literal>)` hit an `unreachable!()` in the planner, and now gets a clean error. This includes a `$param` label, which also crashed before.

## Tests

- **New flow tests** in `test_query_validation.py`:
  - `test47`: inline properties.
  - `test48`: clause expressions (including REMOVE), UNION, trailing `CALL {}`, fulltext, MERGE.
  - `test49`: `ORDER BY`.
  - `test50`: unit-subquery cardinality.
  - `test51`: loop-variable comprehensions via nested plans.

  Plus `test15` in `test_load_csv.py`. Each one fails without its fix: a server crash for the crash cases, and a wrong result or error for the others.
- **Sweep:** 129 queries across every position I could find, run against the fixed build, with zero crashes. Results were checked by hand on a small graph.
- **Full flow suite:** 1593/1593 passed. `test_effects_ddl…ConstraintSettlingRaces.test02` failed intermittently in two earlier full runs, one of them on code from before these changes. It passes 3/3 in isolation, so it's a timing test that is sensitive to load.
- **TCK, e2e, functions, MVCC and concurrency suites:** all pass.
- **`cargo test -p graph`:** 420 passed and 1 failed. The failure is `batched_result_emitter::tests::cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, which fails the same way on `main`.
- **fmt and clippy:** fmt is clean, and clippy only warns in files this PR doesn't touch.

## Note on the triage comment

The triage comment says the empty-graph query "returns a row `1`". That `1` is the column header (`RETURN 1` names its column `1`). There are zero rows, which is correct.

## Nested plans (Neo4j's approach)

A pattern comprehension that reads a variable bound inside the expression around it can't be hoisted, because that variable only exists inside the loop. Examples are a list-comprehension variable, a quantifier variable, or `reduce`'s iterator or accumulator. Before this PR it was hoisted anyway and evaluated once, before the loop, so results were silently wrong. C is wrong the same way when the variable is in the pattern, and errors when it's only in the WHERE or result.

This PR does what Neo4j does with nested plan expressions:

- **Expression node.** `ExprIR::NestedPlan` names a sub-plan. The evaluator runs it each time the expression is evaluated, with the current row (loop bindings included) as the argument row, and reads back the list its keyless collect produces.
- **Referenced variables.** Its children list the variables the sub-plan reads, so optimizer passes that ask what an expression uses still see them.
- **Plan layout.** The sub-plans sit under an `IR::NestedPlans` root, after the query's own plan. `optimize` treats each child as a separate plan, and the runtime maps ids to plan nodes at startup. EXPLAIN and PROFILE show them under `Nested Plans`.
- **Scope.** Only comprehensions that actually read a loop variable become nested plans. Every other comprehension keeps the hoisted Apply, and queries with no nested plan keep their exact plan shape.

Also fixed: a bare pattern in a list comprehension's WHERE, or in a quantifier's predicate, is now an existence test. In a projection it used to collect the matched paths, so `[x IN ns WHERE (x)-->() | x]` was always `[]` and `any(x IN ns WHERE (x)-->())` was a type error.

## Also fixed along the way

- **`ORDER BY`.** Its comprehensions were planned below the projection, while the binder resolves `ORDER BY` against the projected scope. They're now planned above the projection, below the Sort. Also, a name the pattern shares with a parent-scope variable (`ORDER BY size([(n)<--() | 1])` where `n` isn't projected) is now copied in like any other `ORDER BY` reference. Before, it became a fresh pattern-local variable, which silently made the comprehension uncorrelated.
- **Unit `CALL {}` subquery cardinality.** A subquery that returns nothing emitted each outer row once per row of its body: `CALL { MATCH (n:A) SET n.p = 1 } RETURN 1` gave one row per `A` node, where C gives one row. The body is now drained by a keyless Aggregate, which always yields exactly one row.
- **Review fixes.** REMOVE lowering (CodeRabbit). Yielded columns are marked visited before `YIELD … WHERE` (Copilot; the plan was already correlated, but this matches what UNWIND and LOAD CSV do). Two test hygiene fixes.

title: ci(asan): get llvm-symbolizer from the builder, not apt.llvm.org
body:
## Summary

The ASAN image installed LLVM from **apt.llvm.org** at build time, which fails
intermittently and ejects PRs from the merge queue. **3 of the last 18 `Rust PR`
runs** hit it; PR #2469 was kicked out three times, never for anything in its own
diff. Full diagnosis in #2872.

The whole step existed to obtain one file — `/usr/bin/llvm-symbolizer-22` — that
the toolchain image **already has**. This copies it across the stage boundary
instead, so the runtime stage talks to `deb.debian.org` only.

## Why the builder already has it

`llvm.sh` runs `apt-get install -y clang-22 …` *without* `--no-install-recommends`;
`clang-22` Recommends `llvm-22-dev`, which Depends on `llvm-22` — the package that
ships the symbolizer, and the `llvm-objcopy-22` the builder stage already uses:

```
$ docker run --rm ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build:latest \
    sh -c 'dpkg -S /usr/bin/llvm-symbolizer-22'
llvm-22: /usr/bin/llvm-symbolizer-22
```

The runtime stage couldn't see it only because it's a separate stage
(`FROM debian:trixie-slim`).

## Changes

- Drop `wget`/`gnupg`/`lsb-release`, the `llvm.sh` fetch, the `apt.llvm.org` repo
  and `llvm-22` — **four round-trips to one third-party host, gone**.
- `COPY --from=builder` the symbolizer (101 KB) and the `libLLVM.so.22.1` it links
  (143 MB), preserving the `/usr/lib/llvm-22/{bin,lib}` layout. Its `RUNPATH` is
  `$ORIGIN/../lib`, so it is self-locating — no `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, no `ldconfig`,
  no multiarch path to get wrong.
- Add the libLLVM runtime closure explicitly from Debian: `libcurl4` for the binary,
  `libedit2 libffi8 libxml2 libz3-4 libzstd1 zlib1g` for the library.
- `RUN llvm-symbolizer --version` as a build-time smoke test. `apt` used to resolve
  that closure for us; this makes a stale list fail the build loudly instead of
  silently degrading ASAN output to raw addresses at test time.
- Point `ASAN_SYMBOLIZER_PATH` at `/usr/lib/llvm-22/bin/llvm-symbolizer`.

## Testing

Built a probe image with the new `apt` list + `COPY` lines **verbatim** on the same
`debian:trixie-slim` base, then ran a real sanitizer trace through it — an
ASAN-instrumented binary compiled with `clang-22` in the toolchain image, executed
in the probe image:

```
==1==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0xfc1fbdde001d
WRITE of size 1 at 0xfc1fbdde001d thread T0
    #0 0xaaaab5620b14 in main /w/boom.c:4:11
…
allocated by thread T0 here:
    #1 0xaaaab5620ac4 in main /w/boom.c:3:23
```

Full `file:line:column` symbolization. The first probe attempt **failed** on a
missing `libedit.so.2` — that is how the dependency list above was derived, and why
the smoke test is in the Dockerfile.

The full ASAN image build is this PR's own `build-rc-asan-image` job; the stage's
other steps are unchanged.

## Memory / Performance Impact

Measured on the isolated stage (same base, only the `apt`/`COPY` portion, arm64
locally — CI builds amd64, so exact figures will differ):

| | image |
|---|---|
| before | **1.22 GB** |
| after | **301 MB** |

~920 MB smaller. The old `llvm.sh 22` pulled `clang-22`, `lldb-22`, `lld-22` and
`clangd-22` into a runtime image that never compiles anything — its default package
set, which the `apt-get purge` (wget/gnupg/lsb-release only) never removed — plus
~90 MB of unused `llvm-22` tools. Only the 143 MB `libLLVM` and the 101 KB binary
remain.

## Related Issues

Closes #2872

Not addressed here: `build/Dockerfile:74` has the same unpinned `apt.llvm.org`
pattern, but that image is prebuilt and cached in ghcr, so it is hit far less often.
Worth hardening separately.

title: Seek by id: accept compound value expressions opposite ID(n)
body:
Resolve: #2871

The seek-by-id optimizer recognized the ID(n) side of a filter by AST node type (AR_EXP_OP vs AR_EXP_OPERAND), so it only reduced a scan+filter to a NodeByIdSeek when the value compared against ID(n) was a bare operand (constant, parameter, or variable). A compound expression such as x + 1 is itself an AR_EXP_OP, so both sides were operations and the filter was not recognized, leaving a full scan + filter, e.g.:

  UNWIND range(0,10) AS x MATCH (a) WHERE ID(a) = x + 1 RETURN a

Recognize the ID(n) side by the scanned alias instead: the scanned node must be referenced on exactly one side, that side must be exactly ID(n), and the other side is taken as the value expression - which is then guaranteed to be independent of the scanned node and hence resolvable from the incoming record. The NodeByIdSeek op already evaluates its range expression per record, so no runtime changes are needed.

This enables the optimization for value expressions over upstream variables (ID(a) = x + 1), previously resolved nodes (WITH a MATCH (b) WHERE ID(b) = ID(a) + 1), reversed operands, inequalities and multi-bound ranges, and the label-scan variant, while still rejecting self-referential filters such as ID(a) = a.v.

Add flow-test coverage in test_node_by_id.py.

title: feat(effects): let v3 index records name several schema entities
body:
Closes #2866

## What changed

`CREATE_INDEX` and `DROP_INDEX` now name *n* schema entities instead of one. In the record head, straight after the `u32` schema tag:

```
was:  u32 label_id · string label
now:  u16 n · (u32 id, string name) × n      // n >= 1, sorted ascending by id
```

Everything from `u32 field_type` onward is byte-identical, and the position in the record is unchanged.

Id *and* name per entry, never a bare id, for the reason the attribute refs already work that way: the replica verifies the id against the name rather than trusting it. The count is guarded before allocating, as `IndexFields` already was.

Both records, symmetrically — a create that can name several entities and a drop that cannot would leave such an index undroppable over the wire.

**Attributes needed no change.** `fields` has been a list since the codec landed, per statement rather than per field; issue section 2 records what was verified and why it must stay that way.

## Unknown `field_type` bits are now refused

Previously ignored, which was not inert: the bits gate conditional sections of the options block, so a bit this build did not know meant the block was read one section short and the *next* record was parsed from inside this one. Where it did not — a drop carries no options — `index_type_of` called the unknown type a range index. Either way, a future C emitting CCH at a replica that predates it produced a misparse or a silently wrong index; it is now a clean refusal and a resync.

Known mask is `INDEX_FLD_KNOWN = 0x1F`, pinned by a test so widening it is a deliberate edit rather than a side effect. The writer is held to the same rule: this build will not emit a bit it could not read back.

## Ordering contract

Stated in both directions, because it is the one property a conformance fixture cannot arbitrate — a generated fixture is already in some order, so a corpus run passes whether the decoder enforces or tolerates.

> An encoder **MUST** sort ascending by id, so two engines agreeing on the set produce identical bytes. A decoder **MUST** accept any order, and keeps it as sent; re-encoding is what canonicalises.

Tolerant on purpose. Requiring ascending at decode is exactly what makes C's written-order attribute ids resync a Rust replica forever while C-to-C looks healthy. The attribute list has a reason this one lacks — its ids are positional against the value rows and `insert_attrs_rows` binary-searches the span — whereas every entry here carries its own id and name, so order is presentation.

## Version

`EFFECTS_VERSION` stays 3. v3 is in no tagged release, C master is still `EFFECTS_VERSION 2` with no v3 reader, and C's v3 branches are unmerged — so there is no deployed reader for this layout change to break, and a bump would document a compatibility story that does not exist. C's branches absorb the layout change before they merge; raising their version ceiling is not the gate.

## Apply

This build still applies only single-entity index records, because `Graph::create_index` takes one label. A record naming more is refused by name (`ApplyError::MultiSchemaIndexUnsupported`) rather than applied to its first entry, which would leave a replica indexing a subset of what the primary indexed with nothing to say so. The wire is ready for the new index type; the engine says plainly that it is not.

## Testing

176 `effects::v3` tests, up from 166. Every new guard was mutation-tested — removed on purpose, and the matching test confirmed to fail:

| guard removed | result |
|---|---|
| decode unknown-bit check | 2 tests fail |
| encode unknown-bit check | fails |
| encoder sort | fails |
| empty schema list check | fails |
| decoder tolerance (made strict) | fails |
| multi-schema apply refusal | fails (SIGSEGV — apply reaches `create_index` with no globals initialised, so it is caught but not by its assertion) |

**Flow tests.** All 92 effects flow tests pass on this branch — 18 in `test_effects_ddl.py` including the million-node constraint-race classes, and 74 across the other eight files.

One was added. Every index statement in the effects flow suite named a single attribute, so the record's attribute list — the part that was already a list before this branch — was only ever exercised at length one, and nothing end-to-end checked that both attributes cross. `test03_a_multi_attribute_statement_crosses_as_one_statement` covers create and drop. It is load-bearing rather than assumed: truncating the emitter's `fields` to its first entry fails it with `[['first']] == [['first', 'second']]` on the replica comparison while the primary stays correct — the quiet failure being guarded, since a replica with the narrower index still lists it and still answers queries, just not about the second property.

Two failures in the wider `cargo test -p graph` run, `build_bool_is_iso_and_grb_build_is_not` and `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored`, reproduce with these five files reverted at HEAD and are not from this change.

## Dev AOFs will not replay

Effects buffers are built for the AOF as well as replication (`src/graph_core.rs:767`), and a failed apply under `LOADING` is `exit(1)` (`src/divergence_guard.rs:67-75`). A dev build with `appendonly yes` that created or dropped an index holds pre-list records and **will not restart**. Delete the AOF; it is disposable.

A test pins the property that matters there, over both opcodes: an old-layout record is refused, never misread, whatever the label id was — and refused without attempting the allocation, since `Reader::string` bounds-checks through `take` before copying. Measured across six label ids; the two opcodes do not even fail the same way, because a drop is five bytes shorter and its count guard fires where the create's does not.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

Five fixtures on `origin/effects-v3-corpus` (`rec_create_index`, `rec_create_index_text_partial`, `rec_create_index_vector`, `rec_create_index_vector_partial`, `rec_drop_index`) are invalidated by this change — all five verified refused, none misread. Their committed bytes were correct until now; the generator has not compiled against the engine since `77e9527f9` (9 Sep), so regenerating needs that ported first. Corpus maintenance is separately owned.

title: CCH path index: DDL syntax, incremental maintenance, full RDB seriali…
body:
Resolve: #3151
…zation

Convert Customizable Contraction Hierarchies from a pair of graph-mutating procedures into a first-class, graph-level index.

Index model
- CCHIndex keyed by the full (sorted+deduped relationship-type set, weight attribute); the hierarchy (ranks, shortcuts, up/down adjacency) is internal and never materialized as SHORTCUT edges / rank properties in the user graph.
- db.idx.cch.query performs rank-pruned bidirectional Dijkstra over the index.

DDL
- CREATE / DROP CCH INDEX FOR ()-[e:A|B]->() ON (e.w), sharing a single consolidated create-index grammar rule; index type is parsed as a plain string, multi-relationship-type patterns supported, multi-label nodes in CREATE INDEX rejected. db.idx.cch.create / .drop procedures removed.

Incremental maintenance
- Commit-coalesced dirty tracking (CLEAN < RECUSTOMIZE < REBUILD) with a scoped recustomize kernel (per-edge seed + scoped customize over lower common neighbours) for weight/edge changes, and a staleness valve; topology changes that add/remove hierarchy adjacency escalate to a full rebuild.

Effects & replication
- Dedicated create/drop CCH effects keyed by the full set; missing relationship types / weight attribute are created via GraphHub so they replicate before the CCH effect. Verified across GRAPH.EFFECT replication and a fresh replica FULLRESYNC.

Persistence (RDB v20, edited in place)
- The entire hierarchy is serialized into / restored from the RDB in a dedicated ENCODE_STATE_CCH_INDICES payload; no rebuild on load. Phase-1 triangulation scratch (xadj/adjncy/parent) is freed after build (~113 MB on se_vag). v19 decoder moved under decoders/prev; encoder/decoder bumped v19 -> v20.

Tests
- test_cch.py flow coverage: create/query/drop, key exactness (rel-type set + weight attr, order-agnostic, deduped), scoped recustomize vs SPpaths oracle, edge/node add/delete, memory report, single- and multi-index RDB reload, replica full-sync, AOF replay.

Validated at continental scale (se_vag, 3.14M nodes / 6.45M edges): build ~12s, point-to-point query p50 ~1.15ms, scoped updates sub-ms, RDB reload restores the index correct and live.

title: fix(effects/v3): end a run when a segment reads against it
body:
Closes #2842.

A run is collapsed into one bitmap and read back in a single direction, so every
segment inside it has to read that way too. Two paths put a segment into a run
going the other way, and both return early, before the `continues_run` check
that would have ended it:

* the lone-`Range` step-down rewrite claimed the run's direction only
  `if self.run.desc.is_none()`, so a run already committed to ascending kept a
  `RangeDescending`;
* the ordinary `Range` extension in the hot path grows a singleton into an
  ascending pair without consulting the run, which is the mirror — an ascending
  pair inside a descending run.

Every id survives the collapse and `len` stays right, so the decoder's
cardinality check passes and the buffer applies. An `IdList` is positional — row
*k* belongs to the *k*-th id as written — so two entities exchange values on the
replica with no error, no log and no resync. A state-only comparison calls it
green.

## Measured end to end

A primary/replica pair, same workload both ways, the replica taking three
`GRAPH.EFFECT` and no verbatim command either time:

```
before   master mispaired 0   replica mispaired 2   [[4, 5], [5, 4]]
after    master mispaired 0   replica mispaired 0
```

## The fix

One rule: a segment may take a direction only inside a run reading the same way,
and where it cannot, the run ends at that segment.

It is applied where a segment *acquires* a direction rather than where it is
charged. The charge point does observe the mirror case — but it cannot act
before the collapse, which is the actual argument for the earlier placement.

`restart` clears the direction, so the new run's direction is set at the same
moment; leaving it for the next push to decide reproduces the same bug one
segment further along.

## Cross-engine

C carried an independently written version of the same rule. A differential run
found the two designs diverged on a restarted run whose head is a two-id range —
order preserved on both sides, bytes different. C ported this structure. The two
builders now agree on 3,404 sequences with zero segmentation differences, and
this file reproduces those dumps exactly.

The 39-fixture conformance corpus is unaffected: all 36 id sequences in it encode
identically before and after.

## Tests

They assert the pairing, not the population. The id set, the count and `len` are
each blind to this by construction, and the pre-existing
`a_reversal_ends_a_run_rather_than_extending_it` passes on the unfixed builder
because it asserts the segment's *kind* — the property that matters is the
segment's direction relative to the run.

* `a_reversal_inside_a_run_does_not_reorder_the_ids` — a reversal at every
  position of a run long enough to collapse, both directions, through encode and
  decode.
* `a_restarted_run_head_is_folded_into_its_bitmap` — the one case order cannot
  see. Moving the restart one index later leaves every order-based test green,
  including the sweep below; only this one fails.
* `push_order_survives_the_wire_for_arbitrary_sequences` — a seeded sweep whose
  distribution is deliberately lopsided. 20,000 *uniform* random walks all passed
  against the unfixed builder, because a balanced walk reverses too often for any
  run to reach the collapse threshold.

All three were verified failing against a real `origin/main` checkout, with the
non-test code asserted byte-identical to main.

`IdSpace` judged id spaces while `Graph` owned the state it judged: two
counters and two recycle bins, moved by twelve raw writes across six
operations. This makes it the authority instead — it owns `live` and
`recycled`, and every id that changes state changes it through a method here.

### What moved

```rust
pub struct IdSpace {
    live: u64,                 // the entity count
    recycled: RoaringTreemap,  // the free set
    entry_bound: u64,          // where the open batch began
    taken: RoaringTreemap,     // what it has taken since
}
```

`Graph` keeps two of these and no counter or bitmap of its own;
`node_count()` and `recycled_node_ids()` read through. `reserve`, `cancel`,
`create` and `release` are methods on the space, taking no state but the ids.

That is the point rather than a side effect: the boundary is
`live + recycled.len()`, so every operation has to move both halves or
neither. A free-set write that nothing counted was #2797, and the
node-id-liveness bug before it.

### The invariant

```text
live + recycled.len() == entry_bound + taken.len()
```

True at every moment and **returned as an error**, not asserted — a corrupt
id space hands out ids that are already live, and a `debug_assert` says
nothing in the build where that matters. Failing is also the cheap outcome: a
write query holds a private MVCC version, so the damage is discarded rather
than published and replicated.

Making it total required a change of meaning. `taken` counts ids the batch
*took* — created, or reserved and then cancelled — because both move the
boundary. Counting only creates made the equation false for every cancelled
reservation, which is exactly what kept `verify` off the write path:
`CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b) DELETE b` reported
`Miscounted { graph_bound: 2, expected: 1 }` on a legitimate query.

With that fixed, the write path is now held to the same check a replica is
(#2839 step 4). It is the one change here that can fail a user's query.

### Batches cannot be left unopened

Forgetting to open a batch was **silent**. Measured by deleting the only
load-bearing call: the entire flow suite passed while
`CREATE (n) DELETE n WITH 1 AS x CREATE (m)` allocated id 1 instead of 0.
Against a C primary that is a divergence in id-reuse order, which costs a
full resync per delete-then-create cycle and which a state-only comparison
calls green.

- `Graph::in_batch(f)` for callers whose batch *is* a scope — a whole effects
  buffer, one `GRAPH.BULK` command. Opens before, verifies after.
- `Graph::roll_id_batches()` for the write path, whose batch is not: it ends
  and the next begins partway through one `next()` of a pull-based operator,
  across many `AtomicRefCell` borrows. Fused into `Pending::end_segment`, so
  forgetting it also forgets to discard the segment's mutations and the next
  commit dies with `node 0 is already live below the boundary 0`.

One residual, stated because it is not closed: a segment whose only content
is a cancellation still fails silently, since a batch that never rolled over
is indistinguishable from a longer one and `verify` passes on either.
Catching it needs an epoch the id space does not have.

### Naming

`Graph::deleted_nodes()` returned the recycle bin — ids free to hand out
again — while `Pending::deleted_nodes` held ids about to be deleted. Two
names, one spelling, opposite predicates, and the same collision in
`is_node_deleted` on both types. Now `recycled_node_ids` / `node_deletes` /
`is_node_pending_delete`. The collision demonstrated itself during the
rename: a mechanical pass rewrote `Pending::deleted_nodes()` into
`recycled_node_ids()` at `include_pending.rs:95`, which is the exact
inversion. The compiler caught it.

### Tests

Two new kinds, both checked against deliberate breaks rather than assumed to
cover anything:

- A **differential test** drives random sequences of every operation against
  a reference model built from plain `BTreeSet`s. It caught an unstated
  precondition — every reservation must be settled before a batch closes,
  because the boundary deliberately does not count reservations (they would
  grow the GraphBLAS matrix dimension `algo_procedures.rs` derives from it
  while leaving its liveness gate off). Now documented and pinned.
- `release`'s two-set contract, which fails if `requested` and `freed` are
  collapsed into one.

Breaks confirmed caught: `reserve` ignoring `taken` (by the model),
`release` skipping the counter (by the invariant), `cancel` not recording
(by the invariant), and the batch shape shifted by one (by `verify`, on the
write path).
